questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. MLOps pipeline
questions.question: A retailer's machine learning operations (MLOps) pipeline promotes any retrained model to production once its code passes unit and integration tests. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Unit tests may not cover every branch of the pipeline code
options.B: Releases are not gated on data quality and model performance results
options.C: Frequent automated releases leave no time for model documentation
options.D: The pipeline relies on open-source tools instead of a licensed platform

questions.key_concept: AI releases need stage gates on data and model performance, not only code tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the release test actually examines: the code, the data or the model's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrained model can behave differently while its code stays identical, because its behavior comes from the data it learned. Code tests cannot show whether the new version is accurate, fair or trained on sound data, so the release needs a gate on data and performance evidence. Incomplete unit-test coverage is a real code-quality gap, but even full coverage would leave the model's behavior untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because coverage matters for software. But the deciding risk is untested model behavior; perfect code coverage still says nothing about accuracy or data quality.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fast releases can squeeze paperwork. But automated pipelines can record documentation as they run; release frequency itself is not the control gap here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tool maturity varies. But open-source tooling can be well controlled; the weakness is what the gate checks, not who supplies the tools.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes fast pipelines cannot document, though they can record artifacts automatically, and D blames the tooling source, which is not a control weakness in itself.
Final two: B beats A because a model's behavior comes from data, so code tests, however complete, cannot show the new version performs acceptably.
Exam cue: when a model is released like ordinary code, look for the missing data and performance gate before production.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.1 (Decide whether the system meets its purpose and should proceed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Affected people
questions.question: A payment app's AI model automatically freezes accounts it flags as fraudulent, and affected customers can reach only a chatbot that restates the decision. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the model's flagging threshold to reduce wrongful freezes
options.B: Have the vendor certify the model's false-positive rate annually
options.C: Publish a plain-language notice explaining how the model works
options.D: Provide an appeal to staff with authority to reverse freezes

questions.key_concept: People affected by high-impact automated decisions need an appeal route to a human who can override.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a wrongly affected customer can actually do to get the outcome changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Freezing an account harms a customer directly, so people affected by an automated decision need a route to a person who can review and reverse it. That appeal route also feeds errors back into monitoring. A plain-language notice improves transparency, but explaining how the model works gives a wrongly frozen customer no remedy, so the harm continues until someone with authority acts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer flags mean fewer wrongful freezes. But a threshold change needs its own approval, and wrongly flagged customers would still have no way to object.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds independent. But a vendor's figure is an input, not assurance, and it does nothing for a customer whose account is frozen today.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because transparency matters to affected people. But understanding the model does not unfreeze an account; without review by a person, the harm continues.

tips: Eliminate: A tunes the model without giving affected customers any remedy, and B relies on a vendor figure, which is an input and helps no individual customer.
Final two: D beats C because an appeal to someone with authority can correct a wrong decision; a notice explains the model but changes nothing for the customer.
Exam cue: when AI decisions directly harm people, look for an appeal route to a human with authority to override.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Validation evidence
questions.question: A ride-hailing company's driver-deactivation model shows 94% overall precision in validation, yet most wrongful-deactivation complaints come from one demographic group of drivers. Which additional test result should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: Error rates broken out by driver age, gender and region
options.B: Precision on a recent out-of-time sample of deactivations
options.C: Overall accuracy recalculated on the model's training data
options.D: Benchmark results for the same algorithm on a public dataset

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing compares error rates across groups; a single overall metric can hide unequal harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose errors an overall figure might be hiding.
questions.correct_explanation: Deactivation removes drivers' income, and complaints concentrated in one group suggest errors do not fall evenly. A strong overall figure can hide much worse error rates for some ages, genders or regions, which only a breakdown by group reveals. An out-of-time sample checks whether performance holds on newer data, which matters too, but it still reports one overall number and could hide the same group gaps.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recent data guards against drift and leakage. But it still yields one overall figure, which can hide poor results for particular groups of drivers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is easy to produce. But scores on training data measure memory, not performance, and overstate how the model treats new cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because public benchmarks are independent. But they measure the algorithm on other data, not this model's effect on this company's drivers.

tips: Eliminate: C scores the model on data it learned from, which inflates results, and D measures the algorithm on someone else's data, not this company's drivers.
Final two: A beats B because only a group-level breakdown shows whether some drivers bear more errors; an out-of-time sample still gives a single average.
Exam cue: when an AI decision affects people, ask for results broken out by group; one overall metric can hide unfair outcomes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Validation roles
questions.question: Data scientists at a savings cooperative built a member-risk model. They present the built-in validation report from their automated machine learning platform as independent evidence. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before deployment?

options.A: Have the IS auditor validate and approve the model for release
options.B: Have the team rerun the platform's validation on an out-of-time sample
options.C: Have validators independent of the builders challenge and retest it
options.D: Accept the platform's automated report as the independent validation

questions.key_concept: Independent validation needs people separate from the builders; a platform's built-in report runs on the builders' own data, metrics and settings.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose the data, metrics and pass marks behind the report, and whether they had a stake in the result.
questions.correct_explanation: The platform's report runs on the data, metrics and thresholds the builders configured, so it is self-review in automated form: their assumptions shape both the model and its test. Validators independent of the builders, who challenge the design and data and retest, give management credible evidence. Rerunning the platform on an out-of-time sample is a stronger test, but the same builders still choose what is checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because auditors are independent. But validating and approving the model would make the IS auditor part of the control and impair independence; management arranges validation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because out-of-time testing is sound practice. But the builders still choose the data, metrics and pass marks, so the lack of independence remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because system-generated evidence is often more reliable. But the platform tests what the builders configured; automation does not make their choices independent.

tips: Eliminate: A has the IS auditor validating and approving a model, which impairs independence, and D treats tool output as independent, though the builders configured it.
Final two: C beats B because independence from the builders is what makes validation credible; a better test sample still leaves the builders choosing what is checked.
Exam cue: an automated validation report is only as independent as the people who configured it; the IS auditor assesses validation but never performs or approves it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Oversight design
questions.question: An aid agency in Jordan lets a model automatically stop about 30 families' food vouchers a week when it flags duplicate registrations. A supervisor reviews weekly totals. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a caseworker approve each stop before it takes effect
options.B: Have the supervisor review a sample of stops each week
options.C: Rely on validation results to justify the automatic stops
options.D: Restrict automatic stops to very high-confidence flags

questions.key_concept: The oversight model must match impact: decisions that cut essentials like food need a person to approve each one before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much harm one wrong automated decision does, and when a person first sees it.
questions.correct_explanation: Stopping a family's food vouchers causes serious, immediate harm, so a wrong flag must be caught before it takes effect. Human-in-the-loop review, a caseworker approving each stop, matches oversight to that impact and is practical at about 30 stops a week. A weekly sample review by the supervisor adds some human checking, but it comes after the fact: most wrong stops go unseen, and those found have already cut families' food.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it adds human review. But sampling after the fact leaves most wrong stops unseen, and any it finds have already cut a family's food.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because validation shows the model works on average. But a strong validation result does not stop individual wrong flags from cutting essential support.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confident flags are wrong less often. But confidence is the model's own estimate; a confident wrong flag still cuts a family's food with nobody checking first.

tips: Eliminate: C treats validation results as a reason to remove human checks, and D trusts the model's own confidence, which can be high on a wrong flag.
Final two: A beats B because approval before each stop prevents harm; a weekly sample finds a few wrong stops after families have lost food.
Exam cue: match the oversight model to impact; when one wrong decision cuts essentials, expect a human in the loop, not just after-the-fact sampling.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Releasing a model
questions.question: A Lithuanian fertility clinic plans to publish its trained treatment-outcome model, built from patient records, so researchers can download and use it freely. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Researchers rebuilding a working copy of the model from its outputs
options.B: Attackers learning whether a patient's records were used in training
options.C: Researchers using the model on patient records beyond its intended use
options.D: Attackers poisoning the clinic's model by retraining their own copies

questions.key_concept: A released model can leak its training data: membership inference reveals who was in it, which for sensitive data is itself a disclosure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what someone holding the model could learn about the people whose records trained it.
questions.correct_explanation: Once released, the model can be queried without limit, and membership inference can reveal whether a person's records helped train it. Being in a fertility clinic's training data discloses treatment, a serious, irreversible privacy harm. Misuse beyond the intended use is a real concern too, but usage terms and a model card can narrow it, while leaked membership cannot be undone once the model is out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because extraction is a real AI threat. But the clinic is publishing the model itself; there is nothing left to steal by copying it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because released models get misused. But usage terms and a model card can narrow misuse, while leaked patient membership cannot be taken back.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because poisoning is a major AI threat. But retraining a downloaded copy changes only that copy, not the clinic's own model.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about copying a model that is being published anyway, and D assumes changing a downloaded copy alters the clinic's own model.
Final two: B beats C because revealing who was in a fertility dataset discloses treatment and cannot be undone; misuse can be narrowed by terms and documentation.
Exam cue: before releasing a model trained on sensitive personal data, weigh membership inference and data reconstruction; the model itself can leak who was in it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.2 (Membership Inference); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Care-hours model
questions.question: A Croatian disability-benefits office's model sets home-care hours. It has exceeded its error tolerance for three weeks, and the data team logged this as a backlog item. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Treat it as an AI incident and triage by impact on people
options.B: Schedule retraining for the next quarterly model release
options.C: Escalate it to the security team as a possible breach
options.D: Have the data team find the root cause before acting

questions.key_concept: Performance beyond tolerance in a decision about people is an AI incident, triaged by impact, not a backlog item or a security matter.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether people are being affected right now, and which process is built to respond to that.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors beyond tolerance in a model that sets care hours for people with disabilities are likely affecting their care now, which makes this an AI incident, not routine maintenance. Raising it as an incident and triaging by impact on people decides how fast to contain it, for example by reviewing affected cases or disengaging the model. Root cause analysis is needed, but leading with it leaves wrong care hours in place meanwhile.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining through a release is controlled. But it leaves wrong care hours in place for months and skips triage and containment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because incidents are often security events. But nothing suggests an attack; AI incidents include harmful outputs and tolerance breaches without any breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause matters. But diagnosis comes after the incident is raised and triaged; meanwhile people keep receiving wrong care hours.

tips: Eliminate: B queues the fault for a routine release while people are affected, and C routes it as a security breach, though nothing points to an attack.
Final two: A beats D because raising and triaging the incident sets how fast harm is contained; root cause analysis follows, it does not lead.
Exam cue: a tolerance breach in a model that decides about people is an AI incident; raise it, triage by impact on people, then investigate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Triage order
questions.question: A South African emergency dispatch center receives four AI incident reports in one morning. Which should the IS auditor expect incident managers to triage FIRST?

options.A: The priority model's error rate on minority-language calls is above tolerance
options.B: The website chatbot was jailbroken, and its insulting replies spread widely online
options.C: The rota-planning model is proposing uneven weekend shifts for night dispatchers
options.D: The transcription dashboard was down an hour, but calls were still handled

questions.key_concept: Triage ranks AI incidents by likely harm to people, then the business; a quiet tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.
questions.pre_read: For each report, ask who is being harmed now, how badly and how many.
questions.correct_explanation: An error rate above tolerance in the call-priority model means some minority-language emergency calls are ranked too low right now, which can delay help to people in danger; it ranks highest on likelihood and impact. The jailbroken chatbot needs follow-up as a security and AI incident, but its harm is reputational and puts no one in danger; a visible attack is not automatically the top priority.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a public, successful attack feels most urgent. But its harm is reputational, while misranked emergency calls can endanger lives now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fairness to staff matters. But uneven rotas are an internal planning issue a person can correct, with no immediate harm to callers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outages are classic incidents. But calls were still handled during the hour, so the impact on callers was small and has ended.

tips: Eliminate: C is an internal planning issue with no immediate harm, and D was a short outage during which calls were still handled.
Final two: A beats B because a tolerance breach in a live emergency model harms callers now; the jailbreak's harm is reputational.
Exam cue: triage AI incidents by likelihood and impact on people; a tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-8 (Incident Response Plan)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Problem records
questions.question: A Costa Rican park service's chatbot told hikers that a closed trail was open. The problem record, now closed, gives 'model hallucination' as the root cause. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reopen the problem and find why the chatbot gave that answer
options.B: Add a notice that the chatbot's answers may be inaccurate
options.C: Switch to a larger model that hallucinates less often
options.D: Keep the problem closed and note hallucination as a known limit

questions.key_concept: 'Hallucination' names a symptom, not a cause; problem management traces it to data, retrieval, prompt or integration before closing.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the recorded cause would tell anyone what to change so it does not happen again.
questions.correct_explanation: Hallucination, which NIST calls confabulation, describes what the chatbot did, not why. The cause may be a trail-status source that was never updated, retrieval of an old notice or a prompt gap, and each needs a different fix. The problem stays open until that cause is found and a fix verified. A warning notice is a fair extra safeguard, but hikers would still be sent onto closed trails.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generative AI can be wrong. But a disclaimer leaves the cause in place, and hikers relying on the chatbot would still be sent onto closed trails.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because larger models can be more accurate. But if the trail data or retrieval is the cause, a new model repeats the error; the cause is unknown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confabulation is a known limit. But a known limit is a symptom; problem management still needs the specific cause and a verified fix.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps the model before the cause is known, and D accepts a label for the symptom as if it were a root cause.
Final two: A beats B because finding the cause lets it be fixed; a disclaimer leaves hikers exposed to the same wrong answer.
Exam cue: 'the model hallucinated' is like 'operator error': a symptom; expect root cause in data, retrieval, prompt or integration before a problem closes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Model cards after retraining
questions.question: A Mozambican bank retrained its ATM cash-demand model eight times, but the model card describes the launch version. The team says updating the card would slow sprints. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Make an updated model card a condition of each release
options.B: Fully rewrite the model card at each annual model review
options.C: Record each retraining in a change ticket linked to the model card
options.D: Have the IS auditor maintain the model card between releases

questions.key_concept: Every retrained version needs current documentation; making an updated model card part of each release keeps it in step with the model in use.
questions.pre_read: Ask which version the documentation describes, and which version is running.
questions.correct_explanation: Each retraining produces a new model whose data, performance and limits may differ, so a card describing the launch version misleads users, validators and auditors about the model in use. Making an updated card part of each release keeps documentation in step. A linked change ticket records that the model changed, but the card would still describe the launch version.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is less work for the team. But between reviews, users rely on a card describing an older model that may behave differently.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a linked ticket records each retraining next to the card. But the card itself would still describe the launch version's data, performance and limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor values documentation. But maintaining it is the team's job; the IS auditor assesses documentation and does not write it.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the card describing an older model for most of the year, and D gives the IS auditor a documentation task the model team owns.
Final two: A beats C because a linked change ticket records that the model changed, while the card still describes the launch version; only an updated card tells users what is running.
Exam cue: agile does not mean undocumented; expect documentation updates built into each model release.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.2 (Continual improvement integrated into AI system updates)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Ended purpose
questions.question: A Bosnian employment agency's model still recommends training courses to job seekers, though the program it was built for ended a year ago. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the model running while its monitored accuracy stays stable
options.B: Retrain the model on the courses the agency offers now
options.C: Delete the model and its training data now the program has ended
options.D: Have the model owner decide on retirement and record the plan

questions.key_concept: When a model's purpose ends, its accountable owner decides its future and follows a recorded retirement plan.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the model still has a validated purpose, and who decides what happens to it.
questions.correct_explanation: A model built for a program that has ended is outside its validated purpose, and the decision to retire, replace or revalidate it belongs to its accountable owner. A recorded retirement plan then covers dependent systems, records kept for challenges, access removal and the inventory. Retraining on today's courses may come later, but it makes a new model that must pass the gates, and only after the owner decides the model has a future.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because stable accuracy looks like evidence. But the model is outside the purpose it was validated for; accuracy on old outcomes cannot show it suits today's courses.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the model useful. But retraining for a new purpose makes a new model that must pass the gates, and it skips the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the program has ended. But deleting the model and its data loses records needed to answer challenges, and skips the owner's decision and dependent systems.

tips: Eliminate: A treats stable accuracy as proof of fitness for a purpose the model was never validated for, and C deletes records a retirement must keep.
Final two: D beats B because the owner must first decide whether the model has a future; retraining for new courses makes a new model that must pass the gates.
Exam cue: a model whose purpose has ended is outside its validation; its owner decides to retire or revalidate it, and retirement keeps the records.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Rollback readiness
questions.question: A Pakistani environment agency's smog-alert model has a documented rollback to version 7, but its feature pipeline no longer produces two inputs that version 7 needs. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep version 7's documentation ready for use in a rollback
options.B: Rehearse the version 7 rollback now and fix what fails
options.C: Have the data team rebuild the inputs when a rollback is needed
options.D: Drop rollback and retrain a fix quickly whenever a release fails

questions.key_concept: A rollback counts only once rehearsed on the current pipeline; the older version must still run with the features and settings it needs.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the older version could actually run today, not just whether a rollback is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: A rollback restores a previous model with the inputs and settings it depends on, and version 7 cannot run on today's pipeline. Rehearsing the rollback now forces the two missing inputs to be restored and shows whether anything else fails, so the rollback is proven before an incident. Rebuilding the inputs only when a rollback is needed puts untested engineering on the critical path while residents may miss smog alerts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because documented rollbacks look ready. But documentation does not make version 7 runnable without the inputs it needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the inputs can be rebuilt. But doing it under incident pressure is slow and untested, while smog alerts may be missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining fixes behavior. But a rushed retrain is an untested change; rollback exists to restore a known approved state.

tips: Eliminate: A documents a rollback that cannot run, and D replaces a known approved state with a rushed, untested retrain.
Final two: B beats C because a rehearsal now restores the missing inputs and proves the rollback works; rebuilding them during an incident is slow, untested work.
Exam cue: a documented rollback is not evidence until it has been rehearsed on today's pipeline.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Embedding model swap
questions.question: An Argentine soccer club's assistant for members searches documents indexed with a vendor's embedding model. After a vendor swap, queries and new documents use a new model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Pin the version of the model that writes the assistant's answers
options.B: Rely on the vendor's testing of its new embedding model
options.C: Reindex all documents and regression-test search as a change
options.D: Track members' complaints about wrong answers for a month

questions.key_concept: Swapping an embedding model changes retrieval; mixed indexes need reindexing and regression testing like any other model change.
questions.pre_read: Identify which component the vendor changed before choosing which control fits.
questions.correct_explanation: Embeddings from different models are not comparable, so queries encoded by the new model match poorly against documents encoded by the old one; much of the library may silently drop out of search. That makes the swap a change to the system: reindex the documents and rerun regression tests on retrieval before relying on it. Pinning the answer-writing model is sound practice, but that component did not change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because pinning controls vendor updates. But the change was to the embedding model, not the answer model; pinning the wrong component leaves search broken.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor tests its releases. But the vendor cannot test the club's mixed index; customers must test updates against their own use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complaints reveal problems. But members may never notice missing documents; waiting for complaints detects harm late.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's testing of its own release, and D waits for complaints about missing answers members may not notice.
Final two: C beats A because the changed component is the embedding model; pinning the answer model protects a part that did not move.
Exam cue: a vendor change to any component, such as embeddings, is a change to your AI system; test it on your own use.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Updates without notice
questions.question: A Zimbabwean safari-lodge group uses a hosted model for booking chats under the vendor's standard terms, which allow unannounced model updates and offer no version pinning. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run regression tests on a schedule and monitor output patterns
options.B: Accept the terms, since a vendor tests its own model updates
options.C: Have the IS auditor review the vendor's release notes each month
options.D: Revalidate the hosted model completely at each annual review

questions.key_concept: When a contract cannot stop silent vendor updates, the owner detects them with scheduled regression tests and output monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the contract lets the group prevent updates; if not, ask how it would notice one.
questions.correct_explanation: Under these terms the vendor can change the model any day without warning, so the group cannot prevent silent updates; it can only detect them quickly. A fixed regression test set run on a schedule, plus monitoring of output patterns such as escalation or refusal rates, shows when behavior shifts so the owner can respond. A full annual revalidation is thorough but would leave months of undetected change between reviews.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors do test. But the vendor tests against its own goals, not this group's booking chats; customers must test updates against their own use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But detecting changes is the owner's operating control, and unannounced updates may have no release notes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because full validation is rigorous. But updates can arrive any week; an annual check leaves months of silent change undetected.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's testing of its own release, and C makes the IS auditor run an operating control the owner needs.
Final two: A beats D because silent updates can land any week; frequent regression tests and monitoring catch them, while annual revalidation comes too late.
Exam cue: when updates cannot be prevented by contract, expect frequent detection: scheduled regression tests and output monitoring.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Rejection notices
questions.question: A Paraguayan power cooperative's discount-tariff eligibility model logs the factors behind each decision, yet every rejected applicant gets the same three 'main reasons', whatever their application showed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check the three reasons against the model's top global features
options.B: Give applicants the specific reasons for their own cases
options.C: Stop sending reasons, since generic ones may mislead applicants
options.D: Refer applicants to the model's vendor for case explanations

questions.key_concept: Explanations to affected people must be local: specific to their own decision and traceable to the log, not the model's global feature importance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the explanation would differ between two applicants with different applications.
questions.correct_explanation: Identical reasons for everyone explain nothing about any one rejection, so applicants cannot tell what to challenge or correct. Each applicant should get the reasons recorded for their own decision, drawn from the decision log, so an appeal can address their actual application. Confirming the three reasons match the model's top global features shows what drives the model overall, but a global explanation still cannot say which factors decided one case.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it checks the reasons are real model drivers. But global feature importance describes the model overall, not which factors decided one applicant's case.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because misleading reasons cause harm. But no reasons leave applicants less able to challenge; the fix is accurate reasons, not none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the cooperative owns its decisions and must explain them; a vendor has no duty to applicants.

tips: Eliminate: C removes reasons instead of correcting them, and D passes the cooperative's duty to explain its own decisions to a vendor.
Final two: B beats A because only local, case-specific reasons let an applicant challenge their own decision; global feature importance explains the model, not the case.
Exam cue: an explanation helps an affected person only if it is specific to their decision and traceable to the log.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Vendor notices
questions.question: A Montenegrin tax office's AI vendor warned an update may put plausible wrong amounts in tax notices, raising no errors. Procurement left the warning unread for nine days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send vendor AI notices to incident intake with named triage roles
options.B: Have procurement check the inbox daily and forward any urgent mail
options.C: Treat vendor notices as change requests for the next release
options.D: Require the vendor to fix flaws before releasing any update

questions.key_concept: Vendor notices about model flaws are AI incident signals and must flow into incident intake with named triage roles.
questions.pre_read: Trace the path a vendor's warning takes before anyone acts on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor warning that its model may misstate tax amounts is an AI incident signal: households may already be receiving wrong notices. Because such errors look normal and trip no alarms, outside signals like vendor notices may be the only early warning. They belong in the incident process, with named roles to triage them by impact on the people affected. Daily inbox checks by procurement still depend on someone spotting the right email.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because faster reading shortens the delay. But procurement cannot judge AI impact, and forwarding still depends on someone recognizing an incident.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the fix will come as a vendor update. But wrong notices may already be reaching households; a release-cycle request delays triage of harm happening now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors should test releases. But no contract ends model flaws; this warning arrived and failed only because nobody who could act read it.

tips: Eliminate: C files a live harm as a routine change for later, and D asks for flawless releases instead of fixing how warnings are handled.
Final two: A beats B because incident intake brings named triage by impact; a faster inbox check still depends on procurement spotting the risk.
Exam cue: vendor notices, complaints and red-team findings are AI incident detection channels; check that they reach triage.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Kill switch readiness
questions.question: An Egyptian irrigation authority's canal-gate model has a tested kill switch to its previous version. That version is the only fallback and reads the same sensor feeds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test the kill switch each month as well as before go-live
options.B: Obtain a vendor attestation that both versions tolerate feed faults
options.C: Rely on the previous model version as the fallback
options.D: Prepare and rehearse a manual way to operate the gates

questions.key_concept: Disengagement needs a rehearsed fallback that does not depend on the model or its feeds; an older version on the same inputs can fail alike.
questions.pre_read: Ask what takes over when the model is switched off, and whether it shares the model's weak points.
questions.correct_explanation: The kill switch hands the gates to the previous version, which reads the same sensor feeds, so a feed fault or a shared flaw would leave no safe way to run them. A rehearsed manual procedure is a fallback that depends on no model, which makes disengagement a real option. Relying on the previous version, option C, is the runner-up: the handover is tested, but that version fails whenever the shared feeds do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tested switches are reliable. But a switch that hands control to a version on the same feeds still leaves no fallback if both fail.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a vendor attestation sounds like assurance. But it is a claim, not a fallback; if the shared feeds fail, nothing safe takes over the gates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an earlier version is a known state. But it reads the same feeds, so one feed fault or shared flaw stops both; a manual fallback does not.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps testing a switch without asking what takes over, and B relies on a vendor's claim instead of a working fallback.
Final two: D beats C because the previous version shares the same feeds and may fail with them; only a manual fallback works when the models cannot be trusted.
Exam cue: disengaging an AI system needs a rehearsed fallback for its work that does not depend on the same model or feeds.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. After rollback
questions.question: A Malawian tobacco auction rolled back its bale-grading model after two days of wrong grades that set growers' pay. Grading is now normal, but those payments stand uncorrected. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Close the incident, since grading has now returned to normal
options.B: Use decision logs to find and regrade the affected bales
options.C: Retrain the model on the affected bales' corrected grades
options.D: Start root cause analysis on the faulty model version

questions.key_concept: Containment is not the end: decision logs identify the people affected during the faulty period so their harm can be remedied.
questions.pre_read: Ask who was affected before the rollback, and how the auction would find them.
questions.correct_explanation: Rolling back stopped new wrong grades, but bales graded during those two days still carry wrong grades, and growers may already have been paid on them. The decision logs show which bales the faulty version graded, so they can be regraded and growers' payments corrected. Root cause analysis must follow, but it fixes the model for the future; it does nothing for growers already harmed by wrong grades.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an ordinary incident closes once service is confirmed. But service is not fully restored while grades from the faulty days still set growers' pay.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses corrected data. But it is an untested change made before the cause is known, and it does not fix grades already issued.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause prevents recurrence. But it serves future sales; growers already harmed need their grades corrected first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats normal new grades as full recovery, though wrong grades from the faulty days still set pay, and C makes an untested change before the cause is known.
Final two: B beats D because bales already carry wrong grades that growers are paid on; finding and remedying them comes before diagnosing the model.
Exam cue: after containment, use decision logs to identify the people affected and remedy their harm.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Hauls removed by a cleaning rule
questions.question: A Mauritanian fishing fleet trained its catch-forecast model after a cleaning rule deleted every haul over five tons as a sensor fault. Trawlers land most such hauls. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain on twice as many hauls, cleaned by the same rule
options.B: Have the data owner fix the rule and restore real hauls
options.C: Raise trawlers' forecasts by a fixed correction factor
options.D: Test the model's trawler forecasts separately before release

questions.key_concept: Cleaning rules shape what a model learns: deleting real extreme cases as errors leaves the model unable to forecast them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the records a cleaning rule removed were errors or real events.
questions.correct_explanation: The rule treated real trawler hauls as sensor faults, so the model never learned what large catches look like and will forecast them too low. Having the data owner fix the rule and restore the real hauls repairs the data the model learns from. Testing trawler forecasts separately would expose the gap, but the training data would still lack the hauls that cause it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But the same rule would delete the large hauls again; volume cannot restore what cleaning removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it offsets low forecasts. But a fixed factor guesses at the error and leaves the model trained on incomplete data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing by group reveals gaps. But it would only confirm this one; the deleted hauls would still be missing from training.

tips: Eliminate: A adds hauls that the same rule would strip out again, and C patches forecasts with a guessed factor instead of fixing the data.
Final two: B beats D because the gap comes from real hauls the rule deleted; a separate trawler test would confirm it but leave the data incomplete.
Exam cue: when a cleaning rule removes outliers, ask whether they were errors or real cases the model must learn.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. One model, three uses
questions.question: A Kenyan geothermal utility's engineering, billing and legal teams use one vendor language model to draft text. IT approved its latest update after testing only engineering summaries. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner of each use test the update on its tasks
options.B: Have IT run its standard test prompts on billing and legal tasks
options.C: Ask the vendor to confirm the update suits each team's use
options.D: Keep the approval, as the three teams share one model

questions.key_concept: A shared model's update is tested and accepted separately for each use, by the owner who knows what correct output means there.
questions.pre_read: Ask who knows whether the new version still works for billing and legal.
questions.correct_explanation: One shared model serving three uses is three systems to test: a version that summarizes engineering reports well may draft billing letters or legal text worse. Generated text has no single expected answer, so the owner of each use, who knows the work, tests on real tasks and accepts the change. IT's standard prompts reach every task, but not as the teams use the model, and IT cannot accept for them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it covers the untested tasks. But standard prompts are not the teams' real work, and IT cannot judge or accept billing and legal outputs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's assurance is a claim and cannot reflect how each team uses it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model is the same. But the same version can work well for engineering summaries and poorly for legal drafting.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a vendor claim that cannot show how each team uses the model, and D assumes one model behaves the same for every task.
Final two: A beats B because each use's owner tests on real work and accepts the change; IT's standard prompts are not how the teams use the model.
Exam cue: when one model serves several uses, each use needs its own owner's tests and acceptance before an update applies.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Face-matching appeals
questions.question: A Sierra Leonean bank's face-matching model blocks account openings and is retrained monthly on its decisions. Each month, 200 blocks reversed on appeal stay recorded as mismatches. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add appeal staff so that reversals are made more quickly
options.B: Relabel overturned cases as matches in the data it learns from
options.C: Require a manager to approve each reversal that is made on appeal
options.D: Send the monthly count of reversals to the model owner

questions.key_concept: A model retrained on its own decisions must learn from appeal outcomes; reversed decisions left uncorrected teach it to repeat its errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the next retrain learns from a block reversed on appeal.
questions.correct_explanation: Each upheld appeal shows the model blocked someone wrongly, yet the case stays recorded as a mismatch, so each monthly retrain teaches the model that its error was right, and similar applicants keep being blocked. Correcting those labels before retraining turns appeals into lessons the model learns from. A monthly count tells the owner how many blocks were wrong, but the training data would still call them right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because faster reversals help applicants. But the model would still retrain on reversed blocks recorded as correct mismatches.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it adds control. But making reversals harder discourages correcting errors, and the training data would still call wrong blocks right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the owner should know. But a count shows how many blocks were wrong while the training data still records them as correct.

tips: Eliminate: A speeds up reversals without changing what the model learns, and C makes reversing wrong blocks harder.
Final two: B beats D because retraining on uncorrected labels teaches the model its own errors; a count informs the owner but leaves the labels wrong.
Exam cue: when a model retrains on its own past decisions, check that appeal and override outcomes correct its training labels first.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Email scanning and injection
questions.question: A Cook Islands pearl exporter's sales assistant reads customer emails and drafts quotes. IT says prompt injection is covered because the email gateway scans every message for malware. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The gateway may miss new malware in customer attachments
options.B: The gateway may skip emails sent between internal staff
options.C: The gateway may pass instructions written as plain text
options.D: Customer emails may hold personal data the assistant keeps

questions.key_concept: Prompt injection is ordinary text that steers a model; network firewalls and malware scans do not detect it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an injected instruction in an email would actually look like.
questions.correct_explanation: Prompt injection needs no malicious code: an email simply contains text, such as an instruction to quote at half price, that the assistant may follow. A malware scan looks for harmful files and code, so it passes that text untouched. Missed malware is a real but separate risk; even a perfect scan would leave the assistant open to injected instructions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no scanner catches everything. But even a perfect malware scan passes plain-text instructions, which is how injection works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because internal mail can carry threats. But widening the scan's coverage still passes plain-text instructions; the gap is the kind of control, not its reach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because emails hold personal data. But that is a privacy question; IT's claim about injection fails whatever data the emails hold.

tips: Eliminate: B widens a malware scan's coverage, which still passes plain-text instructions, and D raises a privacy question that does not test IT's claim about injection.
Final two: C beats A because injection is plain text, not code; even a perfect malware scan would pass it to the assistant.
Exam cue: network and malware controls do not stop prompt injection; look for controls on what the AI may do with untrusted text.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Errors caught in time
questions.question: Pilots at a Maldivian seaplane operator caught 11 weight errors by its load-planning assistant this month. They now check fewer of its figures, and nothing was logged. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Record the pilots' checks as a working compensating control
options.B: Wait to log errors until one reaches a flight
options.C: Log the catches as AI incidents and analyze their cause
options.D: Have the vendor retrain the assistant on these cases

questions.key_concept: AI near misses, harmful outputs caught before harm, are incidents: log them, triage them and find their cause.
questions.pre_read: Ask what 11 catches in a month say about the assistant.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI output that would have caused harm had a person not caught it is a near miss, and near misses belong in incident management. Eleven in a month shows a pattern whose cause, whether data, prompt or integration, needs finding before a pilot misses one. Counting the pilots' checks as a working control relies on every catch, and people's vigilance fades as they come to trust an assistant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the checks caught every error. But vigilance fades as people trust an assistant, and the cause stays in place until one is missed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because no harm occurred. But waiting for harm discards the warning; near misses are how AI incidents are found early.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the errors. But retraining before finding the cause is an untested guess, and the cause may not be the model.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for harm before logging anything, and D retrains before the cause is known, an untested change.
Final two: C beats A because near misses are AI incident signals whose cause must be found; a human catch is the last line, and automation bias wears it down.
Exam cue: an AI error caught by a person before harm is still an incident signal; expect it logged, triaged and analyzed.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Unusual query volumes
questions.question: Over a weekend, a dealer account sent two million slightly varied queries to an Angolan diamond trader's valuation API, then stopped. IT logged it as a capacity issue. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Triage it as a suspected model-extraction incident
options.B: Rate-limit the account to protect service for other dealers
options.C: Increase API capacity so other dealers are not slowed
options.D: Ask the dealer to spread its queries across the week

questions.key_concept: Unusual query patterns against a model, such as millions of slight variations, can signal model extraction and belong in AI incident triage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what someone gains from two million slightly different valuation queries.
questions.correct_explanation: Millions of slightly varied queries from one account fit the pattern of model extraction: someone learning to copy the valuation model from its answers. Logged as capacity, the event goes to the wrong team and is never investigated. Triaging it as a suspected AI security incident brings in the owners who can contain it, assess what was taken and keep the logs. With the queries already stopped, a rate limit only treats it as load.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it limits the account. But the queries have stopped, so a rate limit treats the event as load and leaves what was copied uninvestigated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because demand seems to be the problem. But more capacity serves the copying faster; the pattern points to extraction, not growth.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is polite. But asking a possible attacker to spread queries out helps the extraction continue unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: C adds capacity that would serve the copying faster, and D asks a possible attacker to pace itself.
Final two: A beats B because the query pattern signals model extraction, which needs incident triage; a rate limit treats it as load and investigates nothing.
Exam cue: high volumes of slightly varied queries against a model are an attack signal; expect AI incident triage, not capacity work.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Before a restart
questions.question: A Cayman Islands fund administrator's investor chatbot began quoting wrong redemption prices. An engineer wants to restart the chatbot at once, which would clear its session logs. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restart it now, then rebuild its logs by rerunning prompts
options.B: Disengage the chatbot and save its logs before restarting
options.C: Retrain the chatbot on the correct redemption prices
options.D: Roll back the chatbot to its previous version at once

questions.key_concept: Containing an AI incident means disengaging it without destroying evidence: preserve logs, inputs and version before restarting or fixing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the restart would erase, and who needs it later.
questions.correct_explanation: The chatbot must stop quoting prices, so it is disengaged first. A restart may not even stop the errors, since their cause is unknown, and it wipes the session logs; a generative chatbot's answers cannot be reliably regenerated from prompts later. Saving the logs first preserves who was quoted which wrong price, and why, for root cause work and for putting right any redemptions made on those quotes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is quick. But rerun prompts produce new answers, not the ones investors saw, so who was quoted what is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the wrong prices. But retraining is an untested change made before the cause is known, which may not be the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rollback is a standard AI containment step. But the cause is unknown and may lie outside the model, and redeploying before the logs are saved risks losing them.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains before the cause is known, an untested change, and D swaps versions before the cause is known or the logs are saved.
Final two: B beats A because rerunning prompts on a generative chatbot gives new answers; only logs saved before the restart show who was quoted what.
Exam cue: in an AI incident, stop the harm in a way that keeps the evidence; capture logs, inputs and version before any restart or fix.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Monthly retraining of a tower-fault model
questions.question: A Haitian mobile operator retrains its tower-fault model monthly on all labeled records, including the fixed test set on which it reports each release's score. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Monthly releases may be too frequent for proper change review
options.B: The fixed test set may no longer match current tower faults
options.C: Each release is scored on records it was trained on
options.D: Field crews may distrust a model that changes every month

questions.key_concept: A retraining pipeline that folds the test set into training turns every later score into a memory test.
questions.pre_read: Read how the pipeline repeats each month before judging what its reported scores show.
questions.correct_explanation: Once test records are folded into training, the model has seen the answers, so each release's score measures memory, not performance on new faults. That makes every reported score unreliable from the first retrain on. A fixed test set can also grow stale as faults change, which matters, but a stale yet unseen set still tests the model; a set it trained on tests nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because frequent changes strain review. But automated gates can test monthly releases; frequency is not what makes these scores unreliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fault patterns change. But even an up-to-date test set gives no unseen test once the model has trained on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because crews must trust alerts. But trust is an adoption issue; the question is whether the reported scores mean anything.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about release frequency, which automated gates handle, and D is a user-adoption concern; neither touches whether the scores are valid.
Final two: C beats B because a test set the model trained on measures memory; staleness weakens a test, leakage voids it.
Exam cue: in retraining pipelines, check that the holdout stays out of every later training run, not just the first one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Tuning on restricted candidate files
questions.question: An Estonian executive-search firm's recruiters all use a language model fine-tuned on every candidate file, though many files are restricted to named recruiters. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add an output filter hiding restricted candidates' names from recruiters
options.B: Remove every restricted file from the model's tuning dataset
options.C: Limit use of the model to recruiters cleared for every file
options.D: Retrain the model without restricted files at the next cycle

questions.key_concept: A tuned model can reveal details of any file it learned to any user, so limit its use as tightly as its most restricted data.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can query the model today and what it learned from.
questions.correct_explanation: A tuned model can reveal details from any file it learned to anyone who queries it, so it is as sensitive as its most restricted training file. Until restricted content is removed, only recruiters cleared for every file should use it. Retraining without the restricted files is the lasting fix, but until the next cycle ends every recruiter can still draw out restricted candidates' details.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because names are the obvious leak. But reworded questions can draw out a restricted candidate's salary or situation without a name, so exposure continues.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the restricted source. But the model has already learned from those files, so removing them from the tuning set changes nothing until a retrain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes restricted content for good. But every recruiter can draw it out until the next cycle ends; use must be limited now.

tips: Eliminate: A filters names only, but reworded questions still draw out restricted details, and B cleans a tuning set the model has already learned from.
Final two: C beats D because the model already holds every file's content; retraining is the lasting fix, but exposure continues until it is done.
Exam cue: a tuned model is as sensitive as the most restricted data it learned; limit who uses it until that content is removed by rebuilding.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Archived models and a platform license
questions.question: A Trinidadian vehicle-inspection agency keeps its retired roadworthiness models to rescore appeals with corrected readings, but they run only on a platform whose license ends soon. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Delete the archived models when the platform license ends
options.B: Ask the platform vendor to confirm the models are archived safely
options.C: Document how each model scored so staff can explain appeals
options.D: Keep a way to run the archived models until appeals close

questions.key_concept: Retired models kept for appeals must stay runnable; a model that only a retired platform can load cannot reproduce or explain decisions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an appeal reviewer would need to do with the archived model.
questions.correct_explanation: An archived model that nothing can load is a file, not evidence. Appeals here need the exact model rerun on corrected readings, so the agency must keep a working way to run it until appeals close, such as a supported export or a retained environment. Documenting how each model scored helps staff explain past decisions, but it cannot produce a new score from corrected readings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the platform is being retired. But open appeals may need the exact model to rerun or explain decisions, so deletion removes the evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor holds the files. But safe storage does not make the models runnable once the license ends.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because documentation supports explanations. But it cannot rescore a case with corrected readings; only the exact model, still runnable, can.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes models that open appeals may need, and B confirms storage, which does not keep the models runnable after the license ends.
Final two: D beats C because documentation explains past scores but cannot produce new ones; rescoring appeals needs the exact model running.
Exam cue: archived AI is evidence only if it can still be run or explained; check whether it depends on a platform being retired.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Retraining as a standard change
questions.question: A Bolivian mining cooperative retrains its ore-price model weekly, with the same code and data sources each time. It wants this classed as a pre-approved standard change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Allow it only if each run passes independently approved tests
options.B: Refuse it; send each retrain to the change advisory board
options.C: Allow it, as the code and data sources do not change
options.D: Allow it if the data scientist who ran it signs off

questions.key_concept: Routine retraining can be pre-approved as a standard change only when every run must pass release tests approved in advance, independently of the builders.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each weekly run produces, and what stops a bad one from going live.
questions.correct_explanation: Each weekly run produces a new model from new data, so it is a change, even with identical code. A standard change can still fit, but only if every run must pass performance and data checks approved in advance by someone other than the builders, with rollback ready. Sending every run to the change advisory board is safe but adds a weekly delay without adding evidence the approved tests could not give.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because change advisory board review feels safest. But it adds a weekly delay, and preset, independently approved tests can give stronger evidence for each run.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nothing in the pipeline changed. But new data makes a new model each week, which can behave differently.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the data scientist knows the model. But a builder approving their own release breaks segregation of duties; it is not an independent check.

tips: Eliminate: C treats unchanged code as an unchanged model, though new data makes a new one, and D lets the builder approve their own release.
Final two: A beats B because a retrain can be pre-approved when independently approved tests gate each run; change advisory board review of every run adds delay, not evidence.
Exam cue: a repeated change such as routine retraining can be pre-approved only when every run passes preset, independently approved gates; one-off edits, such as new prompt wording, cannot.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeal outcomes as training labels
questions.question: A Scottish council retrains its model for council-tax reductions on appeal outcomes, used as corrected labels. Most successful appeals come from applicants helped by welfare-rights advisers. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model learns fixes mainly from applicants who had advisers
options.B: Appeal outcomes may take months to reach the training data
options.C: Advisers may learn how to game the model's decisions
options.D: Corrected labels may lower the model's overall accuracy

questions.key_concept: Appeal outcomes used as labels correct errors only for people who appeal, so the model may keep its errors against those who cannot.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose wrong decisions ever reach the appeal process.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeal outcomes are an incomplete label source: they correct errors only for people who appeal and win, and here those are mostly applicants with advisers. The model learns to fix the cases they bring, while similar errors against applicants without advisers stay labeled as correct. Delay in appeal outcomes slows learning, but the corrections still arrive; the skew decides whose errors are ever corrected.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because late labels slow retraining. But delay only postpones corrections; the skew decides whose errors are ever corrected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because feedback can be gamed. But nothing suggests manipulation; advisers helping applicants appeal is the process working.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because label changes can shift scores. But correcting wrong labels should improve accuracy; the issue is whose labels get corrected.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes manipulation the facts never suggest, and D misreads corrected labels, which should improve accuracy rather than lower it.
Final two: A beats B because the skew decides whose errors the model ever unlearns; delay only slows corrections that still arrive.
Exam cue: feedback used as training labels carries the bias of who gives it; ask who is missing from the feedback.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A triage model's go-live test
questions.question: A Bermudian hospital's emergency-triage model met its acceptance criteria when tested alone; in use, nurses will see its suggested level and decide. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: Retest the model alone on a larger set of past cases
options.B: Trial nurses deciding with the tool on realistic cases
options.C: Raise the pass mark to allow for nurses' own errors
options.D: Have nurses confirm in training that they understand the levels

questions.key_concept: When people decide with AI suggestions, testing should measure the combined human-AI decision, since deference can make it worse than either alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose decision reaches the patient, and whether that decision was ever tested.
questions.correct_explanation: What patients receive is the nurse's decision with the model's suggestion in view, and that pairing can be worse than either alone if nurses defer to wrong suggestions. Trialing nurses deciding with the tool on realistic cases measures the system that will run. Training nurses on what the levels mean is useful, but it is not evidence of how they decide when the suggestion is wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because larger tests are more reliable. But they still test the model alone, not the decisions nurses make with it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it builds in a margin. But a stricter model test says nothing about how nurses respond to its suggestions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because understanding supports oversight. But a training sign-off does not show how nurses decide when a suggestion is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A enlarges a model-only test, and C tightens the model's pass mark; neither measures decisions nurses make with the tool.
Final two: B beats D because only a realistic trial shows how nurses act on wrong suggestions; training shows what they know, not what they do.
Exam cue: when a person decides with AI advice, test the person and the model together in realistic conditions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A job board's vacancy recommendations
questions.question: An Italian job board tested its vacancy-recommendation model for fairness by comparing click rates: women and men click recommended vacancies at equal rates. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the test, since women and men click at equal rates
options.B: Rerun the click-rate test on a larger, more recent sample
options.C: Compare pay levels of vacancies shown to women and men
options.D: Let users choose whether to see recommended vacancies

questions.key_concept: A recommender's fairness is tested on what it shows each group; click rates reflect responses to what was shown and can hide unequal exposure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model chose to show each group, not how users responded.
questions.correct_explanation: Click rates show how users respond to what they were shown, not what the model chose to show them. If women are shown fewer higher-paid vacancies, they can click at the same rate as men and still see worse jobs. Comparing the pay levels of vacancies shown to each group, against criteria the model owner set, tests the model's own decisions. A larger, newer click-rate sample repeats the measure that hides the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because equal click rates look like equal treatment. But users can only click what they are shown, so the test misses differences in what each group sees.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a bigger, fresher sample makes a test more reliable. But it repeats a measure of user response, so differences in what the model shows each group stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because choice respects users. But it says nothing about whether women and men are shown different vacancies.

tips: Eliminate: A reads equal click rates as equal treatment, and D offers users a choice, which shows nothing about who is shown which vacancies.
Final two: C beats B because the model's decision is what it shows; a larger click-rate sample measures user response more precisely, not what each group is shown.
Exam cue: for recommenders, test fairness on what the model shows each group, not on how users respond to what they were shown.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Open findings at launch
questions.question: A Jamaican lottery operator's red team found three high-severity jailbreaks, still open, in its player chatbot. The red team's lead says the chatbot passes for launch anyway. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Launch if the three jailbreaks fail when the red team reruns them
options.B: Have the model owner decide on the open findings before launch
options.C: Have the IS auditor judge whether the open findings are acceptable
options.D: Launch once a filter blocks the three jailbreak prompts

questions.key_concept: Red teams report findings and the model owner decides on launch within tolerance; filtering known jailbreak prompts leaves reworded ones open.
questions.pre_read: Ask who in this story is allowed to accept the remaining risk.
questions.correct_explanation: A red team tests and reports; it does not decide whether residual risk is acceptable. The model owner, within senior management's tolerance, decides on launch with the three open findings in view and can require fixes or limits first; management formally accepts any findings left open. Blocking the three known prompts looks like closure, but reworded jailbreaks often pass such filters, and the launch decision would still have no owner.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a retest seems to show the risk is gone. But generative output varies from run to run, so a jailbreak that fails once can work later.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IS auditors are independent. But deciding whether the risk is acceptable is the model owner's call; the IS auditor reports and follows up.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the three findings quickly. But reworded jailbreaks often pass a filter built on known prompts, and no one has decided whether the remaining risk is acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts one rerun though generative output varies run to run, and C has the IS auditor judge acceptability, which is a management decision.
Final two: B beats D because a filter on three known prompts leaves reworded jailbreaks open; the model owner decides on launch, within tolerance, with that risk in view.
Exam cue: testers and IS auditors report findings; the accountable owner decides whether residual AI risk is acceptable.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An agent acting for any employee
questions.question: A Philippine outsourcing firm's HR agent, running under an administrator account, updates bank details for any employee who asks, on whichever record they name. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to change just the asker's record
options.B: Review a log of the agent's bank-detail changes each month
options.C: Move the agent to a dedicated service account with HR rights
options.D: Limit each request to the rights of the employee asking

questions.key_concept: An agent acting for users should carry the requesting user's rights; a broad account lets anyone act through it on others' records.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose permissions the agent uses when an employee names someone else's record.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent uses an administrator's rights for whoever asks, so any employee can redirect a colleague's pay by naming their record. Limiting each request to the asking employee's own rights means the system, not the model, refuses changes to other records. A monthly review of bank-detail changes would detect misuse, but only after a salary has gone to the wrong account.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But a prompt instruction can be talked around; the administrator rights still allow any change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it creates oversight. But review comes after payday, so diverted salaries may already be lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents should have their own identity. But a dedicated account with the same HR rights still changes anyone's record on request.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt rule the agent can be talked out of, and C gives the agent its own identity while keeping rights to change anyone's record.
Final two: D beats B because enforcing the asker's own rights prevents the change; a monthly review finds it after the money moves.
Exam cue: an agent acting for users should carry each user's rights, not a broad account that lets any user act through it.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Copied partner web pages
questions.question: A Tanzanian tour operator's assistant quotes lodge rates from partner web pages saved at unknown times; lodges change rates often. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fine-tune the assistant on the lodges' current rate sheets
options.B: Add a notice that copied pages may show outdated rates
options.C: Recopy pages on a schedule, recording each copy's source and date
options.D: Have staff confirm each quoted rate with the lodge before every booking

questions.key_concept: Retrieval content needs lineage: the source and capture date of each item, with scheduled refresh, so answers stay current and traceable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decides how current each answer can be.
questions.correct_explanation: Answers are only as current as the saved pages, and without capture dates no one can tell which rates are stale or trace a wrong quote to its source. Recopying on a schedule and recording each copy's source and date keeps the library current and traceable. Staff checks of each quote catch stale rates, but only as a manual step on every booking, while the undated library keeps feeding stale rates into every other answer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tuning teaches the model the rates. But tuned-in rates go stale just as copies do, and are harder to update or trace.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns customers. But a notice leaves wrong rates in every answer and does nothing to refresh the stale pages.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a call to the lodge confirms each rate. But it is a manual check on every booking, while the library stays stale, undated and untraceable for other answers.

tips: Eliminate: A tunes rates into the model, where they also go stale, and B warns customers while the stale pages stay in use.
Final two: C beats D because refreshing dated copies fixes the source for every answer; checking each quote by hand catches staleness case by case and leaves the library untraceable.
Exam cue: a retrieval library is data. Ask where each item came from, when it was captured and who keeps it current.
