questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A quality filter tested only on English
questions.question: A Welsh broadcaster will clean its moderation model's training posts with a vendor's quality filter validated only on English text. A third of the posts are in Welsh. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Use the filter as supplied, since the vendor validated it
options.B: Test what the filter removes from Welsh and English posts first
options.C: Translate the Welsh posts into English before filtering them
options.D: Skip the filter for Welsh posts and keep every one of them

questions.key_concept: An AI filter used to clean training data is itself a model; test what it removes, by group, before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the cleaning step could leave out, not just how clean the data looks.
questions.correct_explanation: A quality filter learns what good text looks like from its own training data, so one validated only on English may score Welsh posts as poor and strip them out, leaving the model weak on a third of its comments. Testing what it removes from each language first shows whether it can be trusted. Keeping every Welsh post unfiltered avoids that loss but leaves Welsh spam in the data and the filter untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor validated its filter. But that validation covered English only; its effect on Welsh posts is unknown.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the filter was validated on English. But translations lose how Welsh speakers really write, and the model must moderate real Welsh comments.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it protects Welsh posts. But Welsh spam and junk then stay in the training data, and the filter's behavior stays untested.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on validation that never covered Welsh, and C trains on translations instead of real Welsh comments.
Final two: B beats D because testing removals by language shows whether the filter can be trusted on both; skipping it for Welsh keeps the posts but leaves Welsh junk in and the filter untested.
Exam cue: an AI filter used to clean training data is itself a model. Check what it removes, by group, before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labels that wait for chargebacks
questions.question: A Hungarian online electronics store retrains its payment-fraud model weekly; orders are labeled genuine unless a chargeback arrives, which can take up to 90 days. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Weekly retraining may be too frequent for proper change review
options.B: Chargeback data may arrive in formats the pipeline cannot read
options.C: Fraudsters may pose as genuine buyers to learn the model's limits
options.D: The model may learn to treat recent fraud as genuine

questions.key_concept: Labels that mature late make recent records look like the default class, so frequent retraining can teach the model to miss new fraud.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts the stem actually gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Labels for recent orders are not final: any fraud still waiting for its chargeback is recorded as genuine, and weekly retraining teaches the model that pattern, so it learns to pass the newest fraud. Probing by fraudsters is a real threat to fraud models, but nothing in the facts points to it, while the labeling rule mislabels recent fraud every week.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because frequent retrains need control. But cadence is a process question; the labels feeding each retrain are the risk the facts point to.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data feeds can break. But nothing suggests a format problem; the issue is what the labels say, not whether they load.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fraud models do get probed. But nothing in the facts suggests probing; the labeling rule mislabels recent fraud in every retrain.

tips: Eliminate: A is about change-review cadence and B about data formats; the facts point to neither, only to how labels are set.
Final two: D beats C because the labeling rule marks unconfirmed fraud as genuine in every weekly retrain; probing is a real risk, but the facts never point to it.
Exam cue: when labels arrive late, recent records look like the default class. Ask whether training waits for labels to mature.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Prompt examples from the test set
questions.question: A Uruguayan beef exporter's export-rules assistant scored 94% on its 300-question test set; the 40 worked examples in its prompt were copied from that set. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The score partly reflects answers it already holds in its prompt
options.B: The test questions may not match what staff really ask
options.C: The long prompt may slow answers during busy shipping weeks
options.D: Forty examples may be too few to teach it the rules

questions.key_concept: Test questions copied into a prompt as worked examples are no longer unseen, so scores on them overstate performance on new questions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must be true of a test set for its score to predict live use.
questions.correct_explanation: Forty of the 300 test questions sit in the prompt with their answers, so the assistant can repeat them, and the 94% partly measures recall, not performance on new questions. Scores must come from questions kept out of the prompt. Whether the questions reflect what staff really ask matters too, but nothing suggests they do not; the copying inflates the score now.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because test sets should mirror real use. But nothing suggests the questions are unrealistic; the copied examples inflate the score whatever the questions are.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because long prompts add delay. But speed is an operations matter; the risk is a score that overstates how well the assistant answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more examples can help. But prompt examples mainly shape answers; the issue is that test answers sit in the prompt.

tips: Eliminate: C is a speed issue, and D treats prompt examples as how the assistant learns rules; neither touches what the score measures.
Final two: A beats B because 40 test answers sit in the prompt and inflate the score now; whether the questions are realistic is a real issue the facts never raise.
Exam cue: anything a model is shown before testing, prompt examples included, must stay out of the test set, or the score measures recall.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Staged releases of delivery-time models
questions.question: A Mongolian courier's new delivery-time model matched rural and city accuracy on past deliveries. Staging covers 5% of customers, all in Ulaanbaatar. 40% of parcels go rural. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the plan, since rural accuracy already matched city accuracy
options.B: Raise the staged share from 5% to 20% of Ulaanbaatar customers
options.C: Include rural routes in the staged share before full release
options.D: Release to everyone, then roll back if rural complaints rise

questions.key_concept: A staged release is the live check of a model, so its share must include each segment the model will serve, whatever past-data tests covered.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each check here tells the courier about live deliveries.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing on past deliveries shows how the model did on history, even where rural and city accuracy matched. Live rural deliveries can differ from that history, through new roads, seasons or patchy location data, in ways only live use reveals, and a city-only stage gives no live evidence for 40% of parcels. Including rural routes in the staged share checks the model where it will run before everyone relies on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rural accuracy matched in testing. But those were past deliveries; live rural conditions can differ, and the staged release is the only live check before full use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a larger share gives steadier results. But 20% of city customers still says nothing about rural routes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rollback limits the damage. But every rural customer is exposed first, and complaints arrive only after wrong estimates have reached them.

tips: Eliminate: B enlarges a stage that is still all city, and D exposes every rural customer and waits for complaints before acting.
Final two: C beats A because matching accuracy on past deliveries cannot show how the model handles live rural conditions; only a stage that includes rural routes gives that evidence.
Exam cue: past-data tests and staged releases answer different questions. Check that a staged release covers every segment the model will serve.

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A platform's new AI provider
questions.question: A Swedish retailer ranks job applicants with its HR platform's AI. A sub-processor notice shows the platform switched AI model providers, with data kept in the EU. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Applicants may not be told a new provider's model now ranks them
options.B: Applicant groups' rankings may have shifted without any testing
options.C: The platform may raise its fees to cover the new provider
options.D: The notice may not include the new provider's security certifications

questions.key_concept: When a vendor swaps the model provider behind its product, the customer faces an untested model change that affects people.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed for the people being ranked, not only for the supplier list.
questions.correct_explanation: A new model provider means a new model behind the rankings, so outcomes for applicants can shift, including for particular groups, without any change the retailer tested. In hiring, that untested effect on people is the greatest concern. The new provider's security certifications are worth requesting, but they say nothing about how its model ranks applicants.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants should know who processes their data. But a notice changes nothing about the rankings; untested shifts in them are what could harm applicants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because supplier changes affect cost. But fees are a commercial matter, not a risk to how applicants are ranked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor reviews often start with certifications. But certifications cover security controls, not how a different model ranks applicants; untested shifts in rankings are the harm.

tips: Eliminate: A is a notice issue that leaves rankings untouched, and C is a commercial matter rather than a risk to applicants.
Final two: B beats D because a new provider changes the model behind each ranking, and the untested effect on applicants is the harm; security certifications say nothing about rankings.
Exam cue: a vendor's change of its own AI supplier is a model change for you. Look for it in sub-processor and release notices.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals that overturn by age
questions.question: A Malaysian state's flood-relief model rejects claims; appeals overturn 35% of its rejections for applicants aged over 65, against 7% for others. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner investigate the model's errors for this age group
options.B: Add appeal staff so older applicants' appeals are decided sooner
options.C: Lower the model's rejection threshold for applicants aged over 65
options.D: Add age as a model input so it learns older applicants better

questions.key_concept: Appeal reversal rates by group are a warning signal of model error; investigate the cause, not just the appeals backlog.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gap between the two reversal rates measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeals overturn older applicants' rejections at five times the rate for others, which signals that the model makes more errors for that group, and wrongly rejected people who do not appeal are never counted. The model owner should investigate the cause so fewer wrong rejections happen. Faster appeals help those who appeal, but leave the model rejecting older applicants wrongly in the first place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it helps older applicants sooner. But it treats each wrong rejection after the fact while the model keeps making them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would cut rejections for that group. But changing a threshold before knowing the cause may trade one error for another, untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the group. But it changes the model before the cause is known, and using age directly may itself be unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: C and D both change the model before the cause is known, and adding age as an input may itself be unlawful.
Final two: A beats B because the reversal gap signals model errors for older applicants; faster appeals help those who appeal while wrong rejections continue.
Exam cue: appeal outcomes are monitoring data. A group whose rejections are overturned more often points to model error for that group.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.3 Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback (appeal reversal rates by group signal model error for that group). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A gradual conversation
questions.question: A Spanish chemical distributor's product assistant refused every harmful single prompt its testers tried, but staff later got dangerous mixing instructions over a long, gradual conversation. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add the staff's prompts to the assistant's blocked-prompt list
options.B: Rerun the single-prompt tests after each assistant update
options.C: Limit each conversation with the assistant to ten turns
options.D: Test and screen whole conversations, not single prompts alone

questions.key_concept: Multi-turn jailbreaks spread a harmful request across harmless-looking steps, so tests and filters must assess whole conversations.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the testers' single prompts could never reveal.
questions.correct_explanation: Multi-turn jailbreaks build a harmful request step by step, so each message looks safe on its own, and single-prompt tests and filters pass them. Testing and screening whole conversations catches the pattern the attack depends on. Blocking the prompts staff used stops that exact path, but the same gradual approach can be reworded endlessly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it blocks the known attack. But gradual attacks can be reworded endlessly; a list of past prompts misses the next one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because regression tests are useful. But these tests never caught the attack, so rerunning them proves nothing about it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shorter chats limit build-up. But attacks can work in a few turns, and genuine long product questions get cut off.

tips: Eliminate: B reruns the tests that already missed the attack, and C caps turns that a gradual attack can fit within.
Final two: D beats A because the attack lives in the conversation's build-up, which only whole-conversation testing sees; a blocked list stops one wording of it.
Exam cue: if harmful output came from a sequence of harmless-looking steps, test and monitor the sequence, not each step.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0054 (LLM Jailbreak); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3 (Direct Prompting Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (multi-turn jailbreaks need whole-conversation testing and screening). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A flaw in a shared template
questions.question: A Greek museum group traced its chatbot's wrong prices to a prompt template shared with four assistants on other models. The problem record covers the chatbot alone. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fix the template, retest the chatbot, then close the problem record
options.B: Have each assistant tell visitors to check prices on the website
options.C: Retrain the chatbot's model on the correct ticket prices
options.D: Extend the problem record to every assistant using the template

questions.key_concept: When an AI root cause sits in a shared component, the problem record must cover every system that uses it.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with the root cause the trace found.
questions.correct_explanation: The cause sits in a shared template, so the same flaw may already be giving wrong prices in four other assistants, and because a prompt behaves differently on each model, a fix proven on the chatbot proves nothing for them. Extending the problem record to every assistant using the template makes the fix, retesting and closure cover all of them. Retesting only the chatbot leaves four unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix reaches the shared template. But a prompt acts differently on each model, so the four other assistants stay unproven after the change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns visitors. But a notice leaves wrong prices in place across five assistants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model gave wrong prices. But the cause is the template, and retraining changes the wrong component.

tips: Eliminate: B warns visitors instead of fixing the cause, and C retrains a model when the cause is in the template.
Final two: D beats A because a prompt acts differently on each model, so a fix proven on the chatbot says nothing about the other four; the problem record must cover all five.
Exam cue: when an AI root cause is a shared component, such as a template, base model or index, widen the problem to every system using it and retest each.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Retrieval rights that lag the source
questions.question: A Qatari sovereign wealth fund's research assistant indexes deal files with access rights. The index refreshes weekly, so a deal restricted on Monday stays retrievable fund-wide until Sunday. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Instruct the assistant not to quote restricted deals
options.B: Refresh the index's copy of access rights every night
options.C: Remove restricted deals from the index each quarter
options.D: Check each user's current rights at the moment of retrieval

questions.key_concept: A retrieval index holds copies of documents and their permissions; checking rights at query time keeps answers in step with the source.
questions.pre_read: Trace when the index learns that a deal was restricted.
questions.correct_explanation: The index holds its own copy of each file's access rights, so for up to a week after a deal is restricted, anyone at the fund can retrieve it through the assistant. Checking the user's current rights at the source each time the assistant retrieves closes that gap. Nightly refreshes shrink the window to a day, but a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the restricted deals. But a prompt instruction is not an access control, and rephrased questions can still draw them out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shortens the gap from a week to a day. But a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes restricted files. But quarterly removal leaves them retrievable for months after a restriction.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction, which is not access control, and C leaves restricted deals retrievable for months.
Final two: D beats B because rights checked at retrieval are always current; a nightly copy still lags the source by up to a day.
Exam cue: in retrieval systems, the index is a copy. Ask whether its access rights can fall out of step with the source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.9 (Information Security)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labelers who agree
questions.question: A Nigerian music-streaming app's comment filter learns from toxicity labels by six overseas contractors, who agree on 96% of comments. A third of the comments are in Nigerian Pidgin. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Sending users' comments to overseas contractors may breach privacy rules
options.B: Agreement below 100% shows the labels cannot be trusted
options.C: The contractors' agreement may reflect a shared misreading of Pidgin
options.D: Users may dodge the filter by writing abuse in Pidgin slang

questions.key_concept: High labeler agreement shows consistency, not accuracy; labelers who share a gap, such as a language, agree on the same wrong labels.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the labels and what they were able to judge.
questions.correct_explanation: Agreement shows labelers are consistent, not that they are right. Six contractors outside Nigeria may all misread Pidgin slang or banter the same way, so 96% agreement can hide systematic errors on a third of the comments, and the filter would learn to treat Pidgin speakers' posts as toxic. Sending comments abroad raises a privacy question to manage, but it does not corrupt what the model learns.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because comments carry personal data. But that is a privacy question to manage; it does not corrupt the labels the filter learns from.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labels should be reliable. But no labeling reaches full agreement; 96% is high, and the issue is what the agreement measures.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because evasion through slang is real. But nothing here points to it; the stated facts concern how the labels were made.

tips: Eliminate: B demands perfect agreement, which no labeling reaches, and D raises evasion, which nothing in the facts points to.
Final two: C beats A because shared misreadings corrupt the labels for a third of comments and bias the filter against Pidgin speakers; data access is a separate, manageable risk.
Exam cue: agreement among labelers is not accuracy. Ask whether the labelers could judge every kind of data they labeled.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An open model for a chess app
questions.question: An Armenian chess-coaching app's engineers chose an open-weight model for its game-review helper, since the model's code repository carries an Apache 2.0 license. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have counsel check the weights' own license against the planned use
options.B: Confirm the Apache 2.0 license covers the planned commercial use
options.C: Test the model's reviews on real players' games
options.D: Proceed, since an open license permits any commercial use

questions.key_concept: Open-weight models' weights often carry their own license, separate from the code's, that may restrict uses or users; check it before building.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the team assumes from what is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: Open weights mean the model files can be downloaded, not that any use is allowed. The code that runs a model and its weights are often licensed separately, and many weight licenses restrict some uses, require separate terms above a number of users or set an acceptable-use policy. Checking the weights' license against the planned use comes first, because testing effort is wasted if the app may not use the model this way.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Apache 2.0 allows commercial use. But that license covers the repository's code; the weights often carry separate terms that can limit uses or users.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fitness must be shown. But it comes second: tests are wasted if the weights' license bars this use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 'open' sounds unrestricted. But open-weight licenses can limit uses and users; only the terms say what is allowed.

tips: Eliminate: D reads 'open' as unrestricted, and C tests the model before anyone knows the app may use it.
Final two: A beats B because the Apache 2.0 license covers the repository's code, not necessarily the weights; only the weights' own terms say what use is allowed.
Exam cue: open weights are not open permission. Before building on a downloaded model, check what the weights' own license allows.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Offline copies that outlive the server
questions.question: Bolivia's health ministry retired its faulty child-malnutrition screening model and shut its server, yet health workers screen children daily with offline copies on tablets the ministry manages remotely. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Take down the download link so no further tablets receive the model
options.B: Mark the model and its offline copies retired in the AI inventory
options.C: Retrain the model to fix the errors, then reissue it
options.D: Disable the model on every device that already holds it

questions.key_concept: A model retired on the server still acts wherever copies run; retirement must disable every copy, including offline ones on devices.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option changes for the next child screened.
questions.correct_explanation: Shutting the server stopped one copy, but the offline copies on tablets keep screening children with the faulty model, so wrong results still reach families. Because the ministry manages the tablets remotely, it can disable the model on every one now. Removing the download link prevents new copies but leaves every tablet that already has the model screening children with it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops the model spreading. But every tablet that already holds it keeps screening children with the faulty version.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the inventory should show every copy as retired. But a record changes nothing on the tablets still using the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the errors need fixing. But a retrained model is a new model needing validation, and the faulty copies keep running meanwhile.

tips: Eliminate: B updates a record while copies keep running, and C builds a new model that needs validation while the faulty copies stay in use.
Final two: D beats A because existing copies keep screening children; blocking new downloads protects only tablets that never had the model.
Exam cue: retiring a model means stopping every copy, including offline and on-device ones, not just the server.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Review only when the model is unsure
questions.question: A Tunisian social-security fund's model scores disability claims. It sends those below 80% confidence to assessors and decides the rest itself. Its confidence was never checked against outcomes. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Assessors may be overloaded by the low-confidence claims
options.B: Confident but wrong decisions take effect with no one seeing them
options.C: Assessors may defer to the model on the low-confidence claims they see
options.D: Claimants may word claims to raise the model's confidence

questions.key_concept: A model's confidence is its own estimate; if it is not checked against outcomes, confident errors reach people with no review.
questions.pre_read: Trace one claim through each route the process allows.
questions.correct_explanation: Only claims scored below 80% confidence reach an assessor, so confidently wrong decisions take effect with no person seeing them. Because the confidence was never checked against outcomes, nobody knows how many such errors there are, and a disability claimant wrongly refused has no reviewer at all. Automation bias among assessors is a real risk, but it affects claims that at least reach a person.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because workload affects review quality. But nothing points to overload, and it concerns the reviewed claims, not the unreviewed ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because automation bias is a classic oversight risk. But those claims at least reach a person; confident errors reach no one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because claimants could game the score. But nothing points to gaming, and errors need no gaming to slip through.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes an overload nothing points to, and D assumes gaming the facts never raise.
Final two: B beats C because confident errors bypass review entirely while the cutoff rests on unchecked confidence; deference affects only claims a person sees.
Exam cue: when only uncertain cases reach people, ask whether the model's confidence has been shown to track correctness.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Retention calls and false alarms
questions.question: A Spanish newspaper phones subscribers flagged by its churn model. Monitoring treats flagged subscribers who stay as false alarms. That rate doubled once callers began offering discounts. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Calls that kept subscribers are being counted as model errors
options.B: The model may be drifting as subscribers' reading habits change
options.C: The monitoring dashboard may be refreshed too rarely
options.D: Subscribers may find the retention calls intrusive

questions.key_concept: Interventions triggered by a model change the outcomes used to monitor it; a rise in 'errors' may be the intervention working.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern by how well the stem's facts support it.
questions.correct_explanation: Flagged subscribers get a call, and since callers began offering discounts more of them stay. Monitoring scores each one who stays as a false alarm, so the doubled rate may show the discounts working, not the model failing, and could trigger a needless retrain. Drift is always possible, but the timing points to the discounts, which change outcomes after every flag.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a doubled error rate often signals drift. But the rise followed the discounts, which change what happens after each flag.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stale dashboards mislead. But the figure itself is current; what it counts is the problem.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because calls affect people. But nothing suggests complaints, and it does not explain the monitoring figure.

tips: Eliminate: D raises intrusiveness the facts never show, and C doubts timeliness when the problem is what the figure counts.
Final two: A beats B because the rise followed the discounts, which keep flagged subscribers; drift is possible but the facts point to the intervention.
Exam cue: if a model's flags trigger action, outcomes reflect the action too. Check how monitoring treats cases where the action worked.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Broker records in eligibility scores
questions.question: A Polish mobile operator's contract-eligibility model scores applicants partly on data-broker records matched by name and birth date; refused applicants receive only their main score factors. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model without the data-broker records
options.B: Let applicants see and correct the records the model used
options.C: Give each applicant a fuller list of their own score factors
options.D: Publish how the model weighs each kind of record

questions.key_concept: To contest an AI decision, people need to see and correct the data it used; factor explanations cannot reveal wrong records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a refused applicant could do under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Records matched only by name and birth date can belong to someone else, so some refusals may rest on another person's debts. Factors such as 'payment history' cannot show a refused applicant that the history is not theirs. Letting applicants see and correct the records used gives them a real way to contest. A fuller factor list explains the score better but still hides a wrongly matched record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the matched records cause errors. But it leaves past refusals resting on wrong records, and refused applicants still cannot see or challenge what was used.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more explanation helps. But factors describe how the score used the data, not whether the data is the applicant's own.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because transparency helps. But a general description lets no applicant find or fix a wrong record in their own case.

tips: Eliminate: D explains the model in general, not each case, and A redesigns the model and leaves past refusals unremedied.
Final two: B beats C because a wrongly matched record looks like a normal factor; only seeing the records lets an applicant prove it is not theirs.
Exam cue: contestability covers inputs as well as reasons. Ask whether affected people can see and correct the data an AI decision used.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A 1% change that flips decisions
questions.question: Validators at a Mauritian housing agency found that changing an applicant's declared income by 1% flips 15% of the decisions made by its grant model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Small input errors may decide which families receive a grant
options.B: The model may be overfitted to quirks in its training data
options.C: Income may act as a proxy for applicants' ethnicity
options.D: Refused families may not understand why the model refused them

questions.key_concept: A robustness test that shows decisions flipping on tiny input changes means ordinary data errors can decide outcomes for people.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a 1% change means in everyday data entry.
questions.correct_explanation: A 1% change in declared income is within ordinary rounding or entry error, yet it flips 15% of decisions, so whether a family gets a grant can turn on a typing slip rather than its need. That harm to applicants is what the robustness test exposes. Overfitting may explain why the model is so sensitive, but it is a cause to investigate, not the risk to people.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because brittle models are often overfitted. But that is a possible cause to investigate; the concern is families' grants turning on entry errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because income can track protected groups. But nothing here points to it; the stated result is about sensitivity to small changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because grant refusals need reasons. But the result is about sensitivity: even a clear reason would rest on a figure a typing slip can flip.

tips: Eliminate: D raises explainability, which the result does not test, and C raises a proxy risk the facts never point to.
Final two: A beats B because the concern is the effect on families now; overfitting is one possible cause to investigate.
Exam cue: read robustness results for their effect on people. If tiny input changes flip decisions, ordinary data errors decide outcomes.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Replies the portal runs as code
questions.question: A Kosovar ministry's staff portal displays replies from its citizen assistant as web code. A tester got a reply carrying a script that ran in staff browsers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Scan citizens' messages for malware before the assistant reads them
options.B: Train staff to close the portal when replies look odd
options.C: Instruct the assistant in its prompt to refuse writing code
options.D: Treat replies as untrusted and encode them before display

questions.key_concept: AI output can carry attacker-chosen content; systems that display or run it must treat it as untrusted input.
questions.pre_read: Follow the output to whatever uses it next.
questions.correct_explanation: Citizens control what the assistant reads, so they can steer it into writing a script, and the portal then runs that script in staff browsers. Treating every reply as untrusted input and encoding it before display stops any script from running, whatever the model writes. A prompt instruction to refuse writing code is something an attacker's wording can override, so it is not a control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because inputs are often scanned. But the attack is plain text steering the model, which a malware scan does not detect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because staff are the target. But a script runs when the page loads, before anyone can judge how a reply looks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the behavior. But prompt instructions can be overridden by crafted input, so scripts can still get through.

tips: Eliminate: A scans for malware when the attack is plain text, and B relies on staff reacting after the script has run.
Final two: D beats C because encoding at display stops scripts whatever the model writes; a prompt instruction can be overridden.
Exam cue: model output is untrusted input to the next system. Look for validation or encoding where the output is used.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Tool descriptions that can change
questions.question: A Saudi engineering consultancy's research agent uses tools from an outside provider's server. The agent treats tool descriptions as instructions the provider can change without notice. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to ignore odd tool descriptions
options.B: Accept tool providers that hold a recognized security certificate
options.C: Pin approved tool descriptions and review any change before use
options.D: Review the agent's tool calls in a monthly log check

questions.key_concept: Tool descriptions are prompt text the agent obeys; outside tool definitions are pinned, and any change is reviewed like a change to the agent.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agent trusts that someone else can edit.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent treats each tool's description as instructions, so a provider, or an attacker who reaches the provider's server, can change the agent's behavior by editing that text without touching the consultancy's systems. Pinning the approved descriptions and reviewing any change before the agent uses it closes that path. A security certificate says the provider runs controls; it does not stop a changed description reaching the agent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it warns the agent. But a prompt instruction is not a control, and a poisoned description is itself an instruction.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification signals good practice. But a certified provider can still change, or be made to change, the text the agent obeys.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs show what happened. But a monthly check finds misuse weeks after a changed tool steered the agent.

tips: Eliminate: A answers injected text with more prompt text, and D reviews logs weeks after a changed tool acted.
Final two: C beats B because pinned, reviewed descriptions stop a changed tool reaching the agent; a provider's certificate does not.
Exam cue: for agents, outside tool definitions are part of the prompt. Treat changes to them like any other AI change.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A labeling guide with a gap
questions.question: A Belgian broadcaster's misinformation model flagged satire because its labeling guide had no satire rule. Staff relabeled 900 posts, retrained and closed the problem. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have labelers reread the labeling guide before each batch
options.B: Reopen the problem until the labeling guide covers satire
options.C: Search the training data for satire posts staff missed
options.D: Accept the closure, as the retrained model now passes tests

questions.key_concept: If bad labels come from a gap in the labeling guide, fixing the found labels treats the symptom; the guide is the root cause.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option leaves in place.
questions.correct_explanation: The bad labels came from a guide with no rule for satire, so labelers will mislabel the next satire posts the same way and the next retrain will learn the error again. Reopening the problem until the guide covers satire fixes the cause. Searching for missed satire posts cleans more of today's data, but new labels made under the same guide repeat the flaw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets how labels are made. But the guide has no satire rule, so rereading it leads labelers to the same wrong labels.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some satire posts may remain mislabeled. But it cleans past data only; new labels made under the same guide repeat the error.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tests now pass. But the guide that produced the bad labels is unchanged, so the next labels bring the error back.

tips: Eliminate: A has labelers reread a guide that still lacks a satire rule, and D accepts closure while the guide is unchanged.
Final two: B beats C because the guide produces every future label; cleaning past posts fixes the data but not the process that made it wrong.
Exam cue: trace bad AI behavior to the process that made the data. A gap in labeling rules is a root cause; relabeling found cases is a symptom fix.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A vendor score as a model input
questions.question: A Vietnamese bank's card-fraud model uses a vendor score; for each retest, the vendor rescores past payments with its current model, trained on later fraud. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the vendor for an independent report on its scoring model
options.B: Record each vendor score with its payment as it arrives
options.C: Monitor the vendor score's distribution for drift each month
options.D: Have validators rerun the test on another random sample of past payments

questions.key_concept: An input rebuilt after the outcome, like a score from a model trained on later fraud, can carry the answer; keep inputs as received.
questions.pre_read: Trace how each input value in the test data was produced.
questions.correct_explanation: A model trained on fraud confirmed after these payments may already reflect their outcomes, so rescored values can flatter the bank's model. Live, the score arrives before anyone knows the outcome. Recording each score as it arrives gives every later retest the values the model really saw. Another random sample, option D, is rescored the same way, so any inflation repeats.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendor evidence is standard for outsourced components. But a report on the vendor's model says nothing about scores rebuilt after the payments' outcomes were known.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because inputs can drift and need watching. But drift monitoring tracks live scores; it does nothing about retests on rescored values that may carry the outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because independent reperformance on new records is sound evidence. But the vendor rescores any past payment with its model trained on later fraud, so any inflation repeats.

tips: Eliminate: A seeks the vendor's evidence on its own model, not on how retest scores are made, and C watches live drift, which does not touch rescored test values.
Final two: B beats D because any past payment the vendor rescores carries what its model learned later; only scores recorded as they arrive match live use.
Exam cue: for every input, ask whether its value could be known when the prediction is made. Inputs rebuilt later can carry the answer.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Choosing a model that must give reasons
questions.question: A Nigerian film fund, which must give each refused applicant the main reasons, is choosing between a vendor's hosted language model that scores applications and an in-house model. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Choose the vendor, since its accuracy warranty covers the risk
options.B: Have reviewers rate how clear each option's sample reasons are
options.C: Choose the in-house model, because its workings can be inspected
options.D: Make faithful reasons for each decision a requirement for either option

questions.key_concept: Requirements such as giving each person true reasons come before choosing a model; a language model's account of its scoring may not be faithful.
questions.pre_read: Note every fact in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The fund must give each refused applicant the main reasons, so whichever model it picks must produce reasons that truly reflect how that application was scored; a language model's own explanation of its scoring may not. That belongs in the selection criteria first. Rating sample reasons for clarity is useful, but a language model's reasons can read clearly without reflecting how it scored.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a warranty shifts cost. But it does not give applicants reasons, and the fund stays answerable for its decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because samples show what applicants will read. But a language model's reasons can read clearly without reflecting how it scored; clarity is not faithfulness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because in-house models are easier to inspect. But inspecting a model's workings does not make the reasons given to each applicant faithful; the requirement applies to either option.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a vendor warranty as covering a duty to applicants, and C assumes a model that can be inspected will give faithful reasons.
Final two: D beats B because clear sample reasons may still not reflect the scoring; making faithful reasons a requirement means each option must prove them.
Exam cue: in build-or-buy questions, set the requirements, such as explainability, before comparing candidates.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A same-day cutover
questions.question: An Ivorian cashew board plans a same-day cutover to its new nut-grading model, after both models graded last season's stored lots alike for a month. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the old model runnable until the new one's live grades hold
options.B: Proceed with the cutover, since a month of parallel grading matched
options.C: Delete the old model's files and logs, now superseded
options.D: Retrain the old model on new data to serve as a backup

questions.key_concept: Until a replacement proves itself on live inputs, the old model stays runnable as the fallback; past-data comparisons cannot show live performance.
questions.pre_read: Picture the week after go-live before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Both models were compared only on last season's stored lots, and this harvest's live lots can differ, so the new model may grade badly in its first weeks. Keeping the old model runnable until live grades hold gives a quick way back. A month of matching parallel grading is sound changeover evidence, but it came from past lots, not the live inputs the new model now faces.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a completed parallel run is classic changeover evidence. But it used last season's stored lots, and this harvest's live lots can differ.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the new model takes over. But the old model's files and logs are evidence for past grades and should be kept under retention rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a backup sounds prudent. But a retrained old model is a new, untested model, not the proven fallback.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes records that past grades depend on, and D builds a new untested model instead of keeping the proven one.
Final two: A beats B because the parallel run used last season's stored lots; only live grades show the new model copes with this harvest.
Exam cue: retire the old model only after the new one proves itself on live inputs; until then the old one is the fallback.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Routing questions to a cheaper model
questions.question: A German online pharmacy's assistant now sends questions it rates as simple to a cheaper model. That model was approved after passing tests on simple questions. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Track complaints about routed answers after the switch
options.B: Accept it, since both models come from the same vendor
options.C: Retest the cheaper model on more questions the assistant rates simple
options.D: Test how the assistant rates medicine questions before routing

questions.key_concept: When an assistant routes questions between models, its routing judgment is part of the change and needs its own testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the approval tests actually covered.
questions.correct_explanation: The cheaper model was tested only on questions already known to be simple, but the assistant itself decides which questions count as simple. If it rates a question about medicine interactions as simple, the cheaper model answers it untested. Testing how the assistant rates questions covers that. A larger simple-question test sharpens the evidence on the cheaper model, but still never tests the rating step.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complaints show real effects. But they arrive after customers have acted on answers no one tested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one vendor seems one system. But a cheaper model answers differently, whoever makes it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a bigger sample is stronger evidence. But every added question is one the assistant already rated simple, so a misrated medicine question stays untested.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes models from one vendor answer alike, and A learns of wrong answers only after customers act on them.
Final two: D beats C because more simple questions still skip the rating step; a medicine question rated simple reaches the cheaper model untested.
Exam cue: when AI routes work between models, the routing judgment is itself an AI output to test.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Three mills running 'v4'
questions.question: A Ghanaian palm-oil group's three mills each run a fruit-ripeness model. Change records show all three as approved 'v4', yet the mills grade the same test images differently. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the differences, since fruit varies from mill to mill
options.B: Check each mill's deployment log names the approved v4 release
options.C: Identify each deployed model by a hash of its files
options.D: Let each mill keep whichever version grades its fruit best

questions.key_concept: A version label is a name anyone can reuse; a hash of the model files shows which trained model is actually running.
questions.pre_read: Note what is the same and what differs across the three mills.
questions.correct_explanation: The same test images graded differently means something in what each mill runs differs, whatever the records say; a label is a name that retrained or edited copies can keep. A hash of each model's files identifies exactly which trained model runs where. Deployment logs are standard evidence, but like the change records they name the label, not the files.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fruit does vary. But the test images were identical, so the difference lies in what each mill runs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deployment logs show what was installed. But they record the label 'v4', which a retrained or edited copy keeps; only the files show what runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it suits each mill. But untracked local versions break the approved baseline and leave grades no one can trace.

tips: Eliminate: A blames fruit although the test images were identical, and D lets each mill drift from the approved baseline.
Final two: C beats B because deployment logs name the label, which retrained or edited copies keep; only a hash of the model files proves which model runs.
Exam cue: in AI version control, a model's identity is its exact files, not its name.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A rollback target the vendor retires
questions.question: A Danish container line's rollback plan for its hosted customs-filing assistant names the vendor's previous model version, which the vendor retires 60 days after each new release. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep a tested fallback that does not need the retired version
options.B: Accept the vendor's release notes as the rollback evidence
options.C: Rehearse rolling back to the previous version each quarter
options.D: Pin the current version so the vendor cannot retire it

questions.key_concept: Hosted model versions disappear on the vendor's schedule, so a rollback plan that names one is only good until it is retired.
questions.pre_read: Test each part of the plan against the stem's timeline.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan's only rollback target disappears 60 days after each new release, so a fault found later, for example when customs queries arrive, leaves nothing to roll back to. A tested fallback that does not depend on the retired version, such as a manual filing procedure, keeps filings going. Quarterly rehearsals prove the rollback works only while the previous version still exists.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because release notes describe changes. But notes are vendor claims and give the line nothing to roll back to.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rehearsal proves rollback works. But it can only rehearse a target that still exists; after 60 days there is none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pinning controls versions. But a pin holds only until the vendor retires the version.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes pinning stops a vendor retiring a version, and B treats release notes as a way back.
Final two: A beats C because rehearsal only proves a rollback to a version that still exists; after 60 days the plan needs a fallback of its own.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, check how long the rollback target lasts. A plan that names a vendor version can expire.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Settings left at vendor defaults
questions.question: An Australian law firm's deposition-summary tool calls a pinned vendor model version but leaves output length and temperature at defaults; since a platform update, summaries stop mid-sentence. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the temperature so summaries vary less between runs
options.B: Add scheduled regression tests that check summaries are complete
options.C: Unpin the version so newer models handle longer text
options.D: Set every generation setting and keep it in the baseline

questions.key_concept: Settings left at vendor defaults change when the vendor changes them; a pinned model version does not pin its defaults.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed, given the model version did not.
questions.correct_explanation: Pinning fixed the model version, but settings left at default follow whatever the vendor sets; a platform update that shortened the default output length would cut summaries mid-sentence. Setting each generation setting explicitly and baselining it removes that dependency. Scheduled regression tests would catch the next such failure, but only after summaries break; values the firm can set itself should not be left to the vendor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because temperature affects variation. But a higher temperature makes answers vary more, not less, and length is the setting at issue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scheduled regression tests catch vendor-side changes the firm cannot control. But these values are the firm's to set; tests would only flag the next change after summaries break.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because newer models handle longer text. But unpinning invites more unannounced change and does not fix unset defaults.

tips: Eliminate: C trades a pinned version for more unannounced change, and A misreads temperature, which raises variation as it goes up.
Final two: D beats B because the firm can set these values itself and remove the cause; scheduled regression tests would flag the failure only after summaries break.
Exam cue: a pinned model version does not pin its settings. Set and baseline every value you control, and keep regression testing to catch what only the vendor can change.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A simulated portal that never fails
questions.question: An Italian freight forwarder's AI agent books truck slots through ports' booking portals; its acceptance tests used a simulated portal that always answered successfully. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: Test the portal connector's error codes for failures and timeouts
options.B: Rely on the portals' own checks to reject bad bookings
options.C: Test how the agent acts when a portal fails or times out
options.D: Raise the pass mark on the successful simulated runs

questions.key_concept: Agents may retry, guess or report success when a tool fails; acceptance tests must include tool errors, not only perfect responses.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test environment with the live one.
questions.correct_explanation: A simulator that always succeeds never shows what the agent does when a portal errors, times out or returns partial data, and agents can retry repeatedly, book twice or report a booking that never happened. Testing those failures before go-live shows whether it handles them safely. Testing the connector's error codes shows the error reaches the agent, not what the agent then chooses to do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because error handling is classic interface testing. But a correct error code only reaches the agent; whether it then retries, double-books or claims success stays untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because portals validate input. But they cannot stop the agent booking twice or reporting a booking that failed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a higher bar sounds stricter. But the runs never included a failure, so any pass mark measures the wrong thing.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the agent's choices to outside systems, and D raises a bar on tests that never included a failure.
Final two: C beats A because a correct error code only reaches the agent; only failure tests of the agent show whether it retries, double-books or reports false success.
Exam cue: test AI agents under tool failure. Perfect simulated tools hide how an agent improvises when things go wrong.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. One agent reading for another
questions.question: A South Korean trading house's research agent summarizes supplier websites for its purchasing agent, which can issue orders; only the research agent reads web content. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run both agents under one account to simplify monitoring
options.B: Require human approval for orders that rely on web summaries
options.C: Trust the summaries, since the purchasing agent does not read the web
options.D: Filter web pages for known injection phrases before reading

questions.key_concept: Text from one agent that read untrusted content can carry injected instructions to the next; limit what downstream agents can do.
questions.pre_read: Follow the web content from where it enters to where it acts.
questions.correct_explanation: A supplier page can hide instructions that the research agent passes on inside its summary, so the purchasing agent receives web content after all, just secondhand. Requiring human approval for orders that rely on those summaries stops planted text from turning into purchases. Filtering for known phrases helps, but injection wording varies endlessly, so some will reach the summaries.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting for simpler monitoring. But one account gives the web-reading agent purchasing rights, widening what an injection can do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the purchasing agent is isolated from the web. But the summaries carry web content to it secondhand.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filtering blocks known attacks. But new wording slips past, and nothing then stops a planted instruction from becoming an order.

tips: Eliminate: C treats summaries as clean although they carry web text, and A hands purchasing rights to the agent that reads the web.
Final two: B beats D because filters miss new wording; approval stops planted text from becoming an order whatever wording gets through.
Exam cue: in multi-agent systems, an agent's output is only as trusted as what it read. Limit actions downstream of untrusted content.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Purchased standards behind a public assistant
questions.question: A Greek fire-safety authority's public assistant quotes retrieved passages from fire standards licensed for internal use; engineers see no license issue, since no model was trained on them. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Its answers share protected text with people not entitled to it
options.B: Answers may merge passages from different standards wrongly
options.C: Its quotes may come from standards since revised or withdrawn
options.D: Its answers cannot show which standard each passage came from

questions.key_concept: Retrieval quotes stored documents to whoever asks, so a source's license must cover the people the assistant serves.
questions.pre_read: Match each option to a fact stated in the question.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval quotes stored passages straight to whoever asks, so the public assistant republishes the standards to people an internal-use license does not cover, whether or not the model was trained on them. That is a stated fact and the greatest concern. Outdated quotes are a real retrieval risk, but nothing in the question says any standard was revised.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retrieval can stitch passages together badly. But nothing points to wrong advice; the stated license excludes the public the assistant serves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retrieval indexes go stale. But the question gives no revision; it does give a license that excludes the public.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting if retrieval seems opaque. But retrieval tools can, and usually do, record which document each passage came from.

tips: Eliminate: B raises merged passages the facts never suggest, and D forgets that retrieval keeps track of each passage's source.
Final two: A beats C because the license limits who may see the text and retrieval shows it to the public; no revised standard is mentioned.
Exam cue: Retrieval publishes what it finds to whoever asks; check that each source may be shown to that audience.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A hail-damage model's test set
questions.question: An Indian crop insurer's hail-damage model team keeps its held-back test set in the team's shared folder, which members open freely while tuning the model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Make the test set read-only so members cannot alter it
options.B: Enlarge the test set so a few looks cannot bias it
options.C: Have someone other than the builders hold and score the test set
options.D: Draw a fresh test set from training data before every new release

questions.key_concept: A test set stays unseen only if the builders cannot look at it; holding it apart, with outside scoring, keeps it unseen.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the risk the facts describe.
questions.correct_explanation: Builders who can open the test set while tuning can steer the model toward it, even without meaning to, so its score stops showing performance on unseen data. Holding the set outside the team, with others scoring each release, keeps it unseen. Making it read-only is a sound integrity control, but the leak comes from looking, which read-only access still allows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it protects the test set from tampering. But the leak comes from looking, not editing; read-only members can still tune toward it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because bigger samples resist noise. But repeated looks bias tuning whatever the size, so a larger set stays exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fresh data sounds clean. But records drawn from training data are not unseen, so the test would measure memory.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts size to undo repeated looks, and D draws test records from data the model already trained on.
Final two: C beats A because the leak comes from builders seeing the test set while tuning, and read-only access still lets them look.
Exam cue: A test set must be unseen by the people tuning the model; protecting it from edits is not enough.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A model card the platform writes
questions.question: A Hungarian tram operator's machine learning operations (MLOps) platform automatically writes the model card for its track-wear model, listing metrics, data sizes and training dates. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the card, as the platform fills it in consistently
options.B: Reperform the card's metrics from the model's training logs
options.C: Have the model owner record intended use and known limits
options.D: Link the card to the team's sprint notes instead

questions.key_concept: A model card must state intended use, users and known limits; generated metrics alone cannot tell anyone where the model is safe to use.
questions.pre_read: Decide what the evidence is for before weighing how it was made.
questions.correct_explanation: A generated card records what the pipeline knows: metrics, data sizes and dates. It cannot record what the model is for, who may rely on it or where it fails, and those are what users and reviewers most need, so the model owner must record them. Reperforming the metrics checks that they are accurate, but accurate metrics still leave the card without its intended use and limits.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because automation is consistent. But a card that omits use and limits is consistently incomplete.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it confirms numbers already there; the missing intended use and limits stay missing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting in an agile team. But sprint notes record work done, not the model's intended use or known limits.

tips: Eliminate: A equates consistent with complete, and D swaps model documentation for project notes.
Final two: C beats B because checking the metrics cannot add the intended use and limits the card lacks.
Exam cue: Pipelines can document numbers; only the model owner can document purpose and limits.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A vendor's precision figure
questions.question: A Philippine rice institute runs a vendor's pest-detection model at a 0.5 cutoff to catch more infestations, citing only the vendor's 95% precision at its recommended 0.8 cutoff. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Vendor precision may come from pests in other countries
options.B: A 0.5 cutoff will make the model miss more infestations
options.C: The vendor may change the model without telling the institute
options.D: Precision at 0.5 is likely lower and has not been measured

questions.key_concept: Precision and recall depend on the cutoff; a vendor's figures describe its chosen cutoff, not the one the organization sets.
questions.pre_read: Separate facts the question states from risks it only invites you to imagine.
questions.correct_explanation: Lowering the cutoff from 0.8 to 0.5 flags more cases, which catches more infestations but also raises false alarms, so precision at 0.5 is likely below the documented 95% and has not been measured. The institute is relying on a figure that does not describe its use. Vendor testing on pests from other countries is possible, but the question never suggests it; the cutoff change is stated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendor test data may not match local pests. But nothing here says so; the stated cutoff change already voids the figure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting if cutoffs are unfamiliar. But a lower cutoff flags more cases, so it misses fewer infestations, at the cost of more false alarms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hosted vendors update models. But the question gives no update; the 95% figure already does not apply at 0.5.

tips: Eliminate: B reverses what a lower cutoff does, and C raises an update the question never mentions.
Final two: D beats A because the stated cutoff change makes the 95% figure inapplicable, while foreign test data is only a guess.
Exam cue: A performance figure holds only at the cutoff it was measured at; change the cutoff and retest.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A retired model's grades as labels
questions.question: A Spanish property insurer retired its roof-condition model for misgrading tile roofs. The model's past grades stay in a shared label store that teams use for new models. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Withhold its tile-roof grades from training until regraded
options.B: Revoke the retired model's endpoint, keys and service accounts
options.C: Note the tile-roof flaw in the retired model's documentation
options.D: Delete every grade the retired model produced from the store

questions.key_concept: A retired model's flawed outputs kept as labels go on teaching every model trained on them; retirement must stop their reuse.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option changes from today on.
questions.correct_explanation: Grades used as labels teach each model trained on them, so the tile-roof errors pass into every new model a team builds from the store. Withholding those grades from training until they are regraded stops the flaw spreading. Noting the flaw in the retired model's documentation is good record-keeping, but teams drawing labels from the store work from the data, not from a retired model's documents.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as standard retirement work. But the model's grades already sit in the store, so revoking its access leaves them free to train new models.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because known limits belong on record. But teams draw labels from the store, not from a retired model's documents, so the flaw keeps spreading.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the flawed grades. But it also deletes sound grades and the records needed to trace which models learned from them.

tips: Eliminate: B ends access to a model whose grades already sit in the store, and D deletes sound grades and the records needed to trace their use.
Final two: A beats C because labels travel without their source model's documents; only withholding the tile-roof grades stops new models learning the flaw.
Exam cue: When a flawed model retires, ask where its outputs live on as training labels; retirement must stop their reuse.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A vendor update and a refusal suite
questions.question: A Nepali family-planning charity ran regression tests on a vendor update billed as 'stronger safety'. The tests were 150 prompts its assistant must refuse, recent jailbreaks included. All were refused. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Approve the update, since every harmful prompt was refused
options.B: Add sensitive but legitimate questions it should still answer
options.C: Add newly published jailbreak prompts to the suite
options.D: Pin the old version permanently so updates need no tests

questions.key_concept: Updates that tighten safety can make a model refuse legitimate sensitive questions; regression tests need cases it must answer as well as refuse.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the test results can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: The suite holds only prompts the assistant must refuse, so it can show the update is not less safe but never that it became over-cautious. Updates billed as stronger safety often make models refuse more honest questions too, and for a family-planning service, refusing honest questions about contraception is a real harm. More jailbreaks would add to a suite that already holds recent ones, and still could not reveal over-refusal.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the safety cases passed. But they test one side only; the update may now refuse questions the charity exists to answer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because jailbreaks keep evolving. But the suite already holds recent ones; more refusal cases still cannot show wrongly refused questions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a way to avoid surprises. But vendors retire pinned versions in time, and security fixes must still be taken and tested.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a one-sided suite as full assurance, and D assumes a version can be pinned forever.
Final two: B beats C because the suite already has recent jailbreaks and more only retest refusals; only legitimate questions can show over-refusal.
Exam cue: Test both sides of a safety change: what must be refused and what must still be answered.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Generated refusal letters
questions.question: A Bulgarian bank's language model writes letters to refused overdraft applicants. It uses each case's logged top factors and a change-approved prompt. Letters are stored as sent. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Inspect the approved prompt against the bank's letter policy
options.B: Let refused applicants request their logged factors on appeal
options.C: Set the letter model's temperature to zero for steady wording
options.D: Have staff compare sampled letters with their logged factors

questions.key_concept: Generated explanations can misstate the factors they were given, so check sent output against the logged factors, not only the prompt.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence each option would produce.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model can state reasons that differ from the factors it was given, adding or rewording them, and an approved prompt does not fix each output the way a configured rule would. Comparing a sample of sent letters with each case's logged factors shows whether applicants are told the real reasons. Inspecting the prompt checks the design, but generated letters can stray from a sound prompt.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a configured control is often tested once. But generated text varies by case and run, so a sound prompt does not show each letter is faithful.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because appeals expose errors. But it relies on applicants choosing to appeal, and a letter that misstates their reasons may mislead them about what to challenge.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because low temperature steadies wording. But steady wording can still misstate the factors; it makes errors repeatable, not checked.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for applicants to appeal letters that may mislead them, and C steadies the wording without checking it states the right reasons.
Final two: D beats A because a generated letter can misstate the factors even under a sound prompt; only checking letters against the logged factors shows what applicants were told.
Exam cue: Generated output is not a configured rule; check samples of what it produced against its source data, not only the prompt.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Campaign images from a generator
questions.question: A New Zealand health-promotion agency's staff check every campaign image from a vendor's generator for stereotypes before it is published. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test many outputs per prompt for how groups are portrayed
options.B: Rely on the vendor's filter for harmful images
options.C: Add a second staff member to check each image before release
options.D: Add the word 'diverse' to every prompt instead of testing

questions.key_concept: Image generators can repeat stereotypes in who appears in which role; the pattern shows only across many outputs, so test in bulk.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each check could notice and what it could not.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff judge one image at a time, but stereotyping by a generator shows as a pattern across many outputs, such as who keeps appearing as the doctor and who as the patient; each image can look acceptable alone. Generating many images per prompt and comparing how groups are shown tests that pattern. A second checker makes each single review stronger but still sees one picture at a time.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors filter harmful content. But filters target explicit harm, not who is shown in which role.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because two reviewers catch more. But both still judge single images, and the stereotype shows only across many outputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a quick fix. But prompt wording can overcorrect or misfire, and without testing no one knows what it does.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a filter built for a different harm, and D applies an untested prompt fix.
Final two: A beats C because a second checker still sees one image at a time, while stereotyping is a pattern across outputs.
Exam cue: Bias in generated content is a pattern; test many outputs per prompt, not single samples.
