questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A pill classifier's referral rule
questions.question: A Canadian hospital pharmacy's pill-identification model refers photos below 60% confidence to a pharmacist, to catch unfamiliar pills. Validation confirmed every such photo was referred. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept it, since every low-confidence photo was referred
options.B: Validate on more photos of known pills, taken on new wards
options.C: Test it on pill types it never saw, checking referrals
options.D: Refer every pill photo to the pharmacist to be safe

questions.key_concept: Classifiers are often confidently wrong on unfamiliar inputs, so a confidence-based referral must be tested with inputs the model never saw.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the test result does and does not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Classifiers tend to label an unfamiliar pill as one they know, often with high confidence, so its photo may never score below 60% and never reach the pharmacist. Validation shows the rule sends low-scoring photos on; it cannot show that unfamiliar pills score low. Only pill types the model never saw can test that. More photos of known pills from new wards test a different gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the rule worked in validation. But it worked on the scores given; unfamiliar pills may score high and never be referred.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because new wards test generalization. But the photos still show known pills, so whether unfamiliar ones score low stays untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as caution. But referring everything removes the model's value; the fix is to test the referral rule.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a rule shown only to act on low scores, and D sends every photo to a person, removing the model's purpose rather than testing it.
Final two: C beats B because only pill types the model never saw show whether unfamiliar pills score low enough to be referred.
Exam cue: Test a model's handling of the unfamiliar with unfamiliar inputs; classifiers rarely say they do not know.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A credit-score API's threat model
questions.question: A Jordanian appliance retailer runs a store-credit scoring API for franchise stores. The API's threat model covers only web threats, such as injection flaws and stolen credentials. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a penetration test cover the scoring API
options.B: Accept it, since franchise stores must sign in to use it
options.C: Add prompt injection to the threat model's web threats
options.D: Add model attacks, for example extraction and evasion

questions.key_concept: Model attacks such as extraction and evasion use the API as intended, so a web-only threat model misses them; MITRE ATLAS catalogs AI attacks.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option would examine with what the facts describe.
questions.correct_explanation: Franchise stores can query the score legitimately and still extract the model, probe which inputs pass, or game approvals, all through normal API use. A threat model covering only web flaws misses these, so it should add attacks on the model itself, drawing on a catalog such as MITRE ATLAS. A penetration test checks the API for software flaws, which is useful but does not test attacks that need none.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as standard API security testing. But penetration tests look for software flaws; model attacks work through normal, valid queries.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sign-in limits access. But extraction and evasion come from valid franchise stores querying as designed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because prompt injection is the best-known AI attack. But a scoring model reads form fields, not instructions; extraction and evasion are its threats.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts sign-in against attacks valid users can make, and C adds a language-model attack to a scoring model that reads no instructions.
Final two: D beats A because model attacks need no software flaw, so a penetration test does not reach them.
Exam cue: AI threat models add attacks on the model itself, such as extraction, evasion and poisoning; MITRE ATLAS catalogs them.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Liveness tests at account opening
questions.question: A Brazilian digital bank's selfie-liveness model passed tests using printed photos, masks and screen replays held up to phone cameras. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Deepfake video fed in by software, never seen by a camera
options.B: Lifelike silicone masks that are better than those it was tested on
options.C: Genuine customers failing it with low-quality cameras
options.D: Staff approving accounts that failed the check

questions.key_concept: Liveness tests often cover only fakes shown to a camera; video injection attacks feed generated video straight into the app, bypassing the lens.
questions.pre_read: Consider how each option would look to someone trying to fool the model.
questions.correct_explanation: Every tested attack was something held up to a camera. Attackers can now inject deepfake video straight into the app's video stream with virtual-camera software, so it never passes a lens and none of those tests apply. Better masks are a real escalation, but they are the same kind of attack the bank already tests for; injected deepfakes are a whole untested route.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because masks keep improving. But they are presented to the camera, a route already tested; injected video is untested entirely.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a usability concern. But a genuine customer who fails is an inconvenience, not an attack on the check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as an insider risk. But nothing here suggests staff overrides; the question is which attack the tests missed.

tips: Eliminate: C is a usability issue, not a threat, and D raises an insider route the facts never give.
Final two: A beats B because better masks use a tested route, while injected deepfakes bypass the camera entirely.
Exam cue: Check what all the tested attacks share; the attack that skips that shared step is often the untested threat.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Choosing patients for a care program
questions.question: An Indonesian health insurer predicts treatment costs to pick patients for a chronic-care program; daily-wage workers use fewer services, as a clinic visit costs a day's pay. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Treatment costs may rise faster than the program's budget
options.B: Workers in real need may rank low for spending less
options.C: Last year's costs may not reflect patients' current health
options.D: Daily-wage workers' records may be too few to train on

questions.key_concept: A proxy target, such as spending standing in for need, carries whatever shapes the proxy, so groups with poor access look healthier than they are.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learns to predict costs, but the program is meant for patients in need. Daily-wage workers spend less because a visit costs them a day's pay, not because they are healthier, so the model may rank them low and leave them out. Costs lagging behind current health is a real limit of yearly data, but the question gives a stated reason why one group's spending understates its need.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a budget worry. But the concern here is who the model leaves out, not how much the program costs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because yearly data lags. But the question states why one group spends less; that cost barrier skews the target itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because small groups train poorly. But the stated cause is lost wages, which skews costs, not the record count.

tips: Eliminate: D blames the record count when the stated cause is lost wages, and A weighs the budget rather than who the model picks.
Final two: B beats C because spending stands in for need, and the question says daily-wage workers spend less for reasons other than health.
Exam cue: Check what a model's target really measures; a proxy carries every barrier that shapes it.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Copies of rare track videos
questions.question: A Japanese rail operator copied each of its nine track-obstruction videos 400 times, after setting test data aside, so its detection model has enough examples. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Copies may push the model to raise more false alarms
options.B: Copying may lower the accuracy of the videos' labels
options.C: Copies add no new kinds of obstruction to learn from
options.D: Storing 3,600 copied videos may strain the team's storage

questions.key_concept: Copying rare examples (oversampling) raises their count but adds no variety, so a model may learn only those few cases.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: Copying nine videos 400 times gives 3,600 files but still only nine situations, so the model may learn those exact scenes and miss other objects, light or track positions. More copies are not more evidence. Oversampling can also make a model flag obstructions more often, but that is tuned with the alert threshold; no threshold adds the scenes it never saw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because oversampling shifts how often a model flags the rare class. But that is tuned with the alert threshold; no threshold adds scenes the model never saw.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data handling can corrupt labels. But each copy keeps its video's label, so label accuracy is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a practical cost. But storage is easy to add; the risk is a model that has seen only nine scenes.

tips: Eliminate: B expects copying to change labels, which copies keep, and D weighs storage cost rather than what the model learns.
Final two: C beats A because extra false alarms can be tuned with the threshold, while nine copied scenes cannot teach obstructions the model never saw.
Exam cue: More copies of the same rare case are not more evidence; ask how many different cases the model really saw.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A new banner on the review screen
questions.question: A Mexican online bank's release replaced the money-mule score on account reviewers' screens with a red 'Likely mule' banner, approved as a routine interface change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the routine approval, since the model itself is unchanged
options.B: Retest the mule model's accuracy on recent accounts
options.C: Test how the banner shifts decisions on flagged accounts
options.D: Add the banner's wording to the model's documentation

questions.key_concept: How AI output is shown shapes how people act on it, so a display change alters the human-AI system even when the model is unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: A red 'Likely mule' banner invites reviewers to agree without checking, a form of automation bias, so the release may shift reviewers' decisions on flagged accounts, even though the model is unchanged. That makes it a change to the AI system, needing tests of the decisions people make with it. Retesting the model's accuracy is sound practice after changes, but the model did not change; what changed is how people use its output.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because only the screen changed. But the screen shapes how people act on the score, so decisions can shift.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retesting follows change. But the model did not change; the risk is in how reviewers act on the banner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documentation should match use. But recording the wording does not show its effect on decisions.

tips: Eliminate: A limits an AI change to the model itself, and D records the banner without testing its effect.
Final two: C beats B because the model is unchanged, while the banner can push reviewers to agree with flags unchecked.
Exam cue: Changes to how AI output is shown, routed or reviewed are AI changes too; test the decisions people make with it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. One controller and 30 haul trucks
questions.question: At a Swedish iron mine, one remote controller oversees 30 autonomous haul trucks and must take over within ten seconds whenever a truck halts unexpectedly. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the controller approve each truck's moves in advance
options.B: Rely on the trucks halting safely when they are unsure
options.C: Log each takeover for the mine manager's monthly review
options.D: Set trucks per controller from tested takeover times

questions.key_concept: On-the-loop oversight works only if the overseer can respond in time, so set how many systems each person watches from tested response times.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: A controller watching 30 trucks may face several halts at once, so the ten-second takeover may be impossible exactly when it matters. The number of trucks per controller should be set from tested takeover times. Logging takeovers for monthly review is good oversight evidence, but it looks back at events and does nothing to make a timely takeover possible.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval sounds safest. But approving every move of 30 trucks is unworkable, so it would become a rubber stamp.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because halting is a safe default. But halted trucks still need a takeover, which is the gap in question.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because takeover records support oversight. But reviewing them monthly cannot make a ten-second response possible across 30 trucks.

tips: Eliminate: A puts a person in the loop for every move of 30 trucks, and B relies on halting, which still needs a takeover.
Final two: D beats C because oversight must work in real time, and a monthly review cannot speed up a takeover.
Exam cue: Oversight on the loop needs people who can act in time; check how many systems each overseer must watch.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Yarn-strength forecasts after an upgrade
questions.question: For six weeks since a lab-system upgrade, one reading fed to a Pakistani textile mill's yarn-strength model has stayed at the same in-range value; forecasts look normal. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Monitor forecasts for shifts outside their usual ranges
options.B: Retrain monthly so the model adapts to the lab feed
options.C: Compare each input's spread with its training data
options.D: Add range checks that reject impossible lab readings

questions.key_concept: A feed stuck at a plausible value passes range checks and can leave outputs looking normal; comparing input distributions with training data catches it.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: For six weeks the model has used one unchanging reading, yet its forecasts look normal, so monitoring outputs alone would not raise an alarm. Comparing each input's spread with its training data shows a reading that no longer varies. Watching forecasts for unusual shifts is a sound monitor, but the question says the forecasts look normal.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because output shifts often signal trouble. But these forecasts look normal, so a stuck reading would pass unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining adapts models. But training on a stuck reading teaches the model to disregard a real input.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because input validation is a standard control. But the stuck value is in range, so range checks pass it.

tips: Eliminate: B trains on the stuck reading instead of catching it, and D's range checks pass a value that is in range.
Final two: C beats A because forecasts look normal, so only comparing each input's spread with training data reveals a reading that never varies.
Exam cue: Models fail quietly on bad inputs; monitor each input's distribution as well as the outputs.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals decided by a rescore
questions.question: A Chilean municipality's model sets school-transport eligibility. On appeal, families correct their data and the model rescores. Staff may not grant transport against the new score. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send families the model's main factors with each new score
options.B: Have staff check each corrected input against source records first
options.C: Retrain the model on each appeal's corrected data
options.D: Let appeal staff decide against the score, giving reasons

questions.key_concept: An appeal that only reruns the model with corrected data cannot fix errors in the model's judgment; someone must be able to decide against it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change about appeals.
questions.correct_explanation: Rescoring after a data fix only corrects input errors. If the model misjudges a family's situation, for example a dangerous walking route it does not weigh, the new score repeats the mistake, and staff cannot override it. Letting staff decide against the score, with reasons, makes the appeal real. Checking corrected inputs against source records is good practice, but it improves only the inputs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as transparency. But knowing the factors does not let anyone overturn a wrong result.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it guards against false corrections. But it still leaves the model as the final judge of every appeal.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because corrections improve data. But retraining on each appeal changes the model without fixing how appeals are decided.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the model instead of the appeal, and A explains a result nobody can overturn.
Final two: D beats B because better inputs still leave the model the final judge, while staff authority can correct its judgment.
Exam cue: A real appeal can reach a different answer than the model; rerunning the model is not an appeal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A ranking model's launch fairness test
questions.question: An Austrian crowdfunding platform ranks projects with a model retrained weekly on backers' clicks. In its launch fairness test, the model ranked projects by women and men alike. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Ranking should stay fair, as sex is not one of its inputs
options.B: The launch result can stand until ranking accuracy falls
options.C: Backers' clicks are neutral, so retraining is unlikely to add bias
options.D: Feedback from its own rankings can open a gap later

questions.key_concept: A model retrained on behavior its own outputs shape, such as clicks on its rankings, can widen group gaps after launch, so fairness needs retesting.
questions.pre_read: Check each conclusion against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: Backers tend to click what a ranking shows first, and the model retrains weekly on those clicks, so any early dip for one group's projects can mean fewer clicks, lower ranks and fewer clicks again. Each weekly retrain replaces the model the launch test described. Waiting for accuracy to fall, option B, sounds careful, but accuracy measured on those same clicks can hold steady while a gap grows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting if sex is not an input. But other signals, including the clicks it learns from, can track creators' sex.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because falling accuracy often triggers a retest. But accuracy measured on clicks its own rankings shaped can stay steady while one group's projects sink.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because clicks look like plain behavior. But people tend to click what a ranking shows first, so retraining on clicks feeds its own rankings back into it.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a model without a sex input cannot treat creators differently, and C treats clicks as neutral, though people tend to click what a ranking shows first.
Final two: D beats B because the model learns from clicks its own rankings shape, so a gap can grow each week while accuracy measured on those clicks holds steady.
Exam cue: When a model retrains on behavior its own outputs shape, a one-time fairness test goes stale; expect retests after retraining.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A credit validation unit's first chatbot
questions.question: A Jordanian bank's validation unit, experienced with credit-scoring models, plans to validate its first customer chatbot with its usual accuracy, stability and backtesting checks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the chatbot vendor's safety report instead
options.B: Run its usual checks on a far larger sample of customer chats
options.C: Add tests by skilled staff for invented and harmful replies
options.D: Skip validation, as the chatbot makes no credit decisions

questions.key_concept: Chatbots fail in ways credit-model checks do not test, such as invented facts and harmful replies, so validation must fit the model type.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not test.
questions.correct_explanation: Accuracy, stability and backtesting suit scoring models with numeric outputs, but a chatbot fails differently: it can invent facts (confabulation) or give harmful replies in fluent text. Validation needs tests for those failures, run by people who know how to find them. A larger sample makes the usual checks firmer, but it still does not look for the failures that matter in a chatbot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors test safety. But the vendor's tests may not cover the bank's chatbot as configured.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more data firms up results. But the usual checks do not look for invented facts or harmful replies at any sample size.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no credit decisions are made. But wrong or harmful replies to customers still carry real risk.

tips: Eliminate: A substitutes the vendor's testing for the bank's, and D ties validation only to credit decisions.
Final two: C beats B because the usual checks miss generative failures, and a bigger sample does not change what they test.
Exam cue: Match validation methods and skills to the model type; generative AI needs tests for invented and harmful output.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A shared model trained across banks
questions.question: Eight Swiss cantonal banks train a shared fraud model by federated learning; secure aggregation means no one, the coordinator included, sees any single bank's update. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The shared model running too slowly for live payments
options.B: A bank inferring other banks' customers from the shared updates
options.C: Customer records exposed when each bank sends its data
options.D: One bank's crafted updates planting a hidden flaw in the shared model

questions.key_concept: Federated learning shares updates, not records; secure aggregation hides each update from others, which also hides a poisoned update from inspection.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each threat against the design the question describes.
questions.correct_explanation: Secure aggregation means no one can see any single bank's update, which greatly narrows the inference threat. But it also means nobody can inspect any update, so a member that crafts poisoned updates can plant a hidden flaw in the shared model unseen. Inference from updates is a real federated-learning risk, but the stated design is built to narrow exactly that.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a performance worry. But the training method says little about scoring speed, and nothing points to delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because updates can leak training details. But secure aggregation hides each bank's update, leaving only the combined result, which narrows this route.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting if records seem to be pooled. But federated learning keeps records at each bank and shares only updates.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes records leave each bank, and A raises speed, which the facts never question.
Final two: D beats B because secure aggregation narrows the inference route but also hides a poisoned update from inspection.
Exam cue: A privacy safeguard can hide manipulation; ask what each design choice stops others from seeing.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A rise in approved top-ups
questions.question: A Thai ride-hailing app's wallet fraud model is hash-matched to the approved release. This month it approved 15% more top-ups, most from new accounts. Managers credit the rise to fewer false declines. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Adjust the decision threshold to bring top-up approvals down
options.B: Have the owner log a possible incident and check the extra top-ups
options.C: Have the model retested on its original holdout set
options.D: Report the rise as a model improvement to the board

questions.key_concept: A model's outputs can shift with no change to it when its inputs change, as under evasion; triage an unexplained shift as a possible incident.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would do now and what it would leave open.
questions.correct_explanation: The running model matches the approved release, yet it approves 15% more top-ups, most from new accounts. An unchanged model's outputs can shift when its inputs change: fraudsters may have learned what it passes, or an input may be broken. Fewer declines are not proof of fewer false declines. Having the owner log a possible incident and check the extra top-ups finds out now. A holdout retest would only repeat the release scores.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a quick correction. But changing the threshold before knowing the cause is an untested change.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a retest is evidence-based. But an unchanged model scores the same on its original holdout set, which holds none of this month's inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the result looks good. But an unexplained shift needs explaining before it is reported as a gain.

tips: Eliminate: A changes the threshold before the cause is known, and D reports an unexplained shift as success.
Final two: B beats C because an unchanged model's outputs can shift when its inputs change; its original holdout set holds none of this month's new-account top-ups.
Exam cue: An unexplained jump in an AI's outputs, even a welcome one, is a possible incident to triage now.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A tag called 'latest'
questions.question: A Canadian ticket reseller's servers load whichever price model is tagged 'latest'. Nightly retraining moves that tag once tests pass. New servers start as traffic rises. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the last seven nightly models in storage for rollback
options.B: Add stricter automated tests before each nightly tag move
options.C: Have servers use an approved version by its fixed identifier
options.D: Limit new server starts to low-traffic hours to avoid surprises

questions.key_concept: A moving 'latest' tag lets servers started at different times run different models; production should load a fixed, approved version.
questions.pre_read: Trace what the stated setup does over several nights.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the tag moves nightly and servers load it whenever they start, servers launched before and after a retrain run different models side by side, and which model a customer gets depends on when a server happened to start. Using an approved version by its fixed identifier makes each deployment deliberate and traceable. Stricter tests improve each candidate but leave the mixing in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because kept versions allow rollback. But storage does not stop servers started at different times running different versions side by side.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better tests catch weak models. But passing tests does not stop servers started at different times running different versions side by side.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer starts mean fewer surprises. But it gives up capacity at peak times, and servers started on different nights still run different models.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps old models but leaves servers mixing versions, and D gives up peak capacity while servers started on different nights still differ.
Final two: C beats B because a fixed approved version stops servers mixing versions, while stricter tests only improve each candidate.
Exam cue: Production should run a fixed, approved model version; with a moving tag, each restart can load a different model.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Correct refunds in acceptance
questions.question: A Slovenian retailer's returns agent, which can email customers, update stock and pay refunds, passed acceptance because each of 200 test returns ended with the correct refund. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add 200 more test returns to raise the statistical confidence
options.B: Run each test return several times and compare refunds
options.C: Accept the results, since emails and stock follow from the refund
options.D: Review every tool action it took in each test return

questions.key_concept: An agent can reach the right result through wrong actions; acceptance checks every action it takes, not just its final outcome.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for what it would add to the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Checking only the final refund misses everything the agent did on the way: it may have emailed customers wrong promises, sent duplicates or changed stock levels wrongly while still ending with the right refund. Acceptance should review every tool action from the test runs. Repeating each test shows whether refunds vary between runs, which is useful, but it still looks only at the final refund.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more cases add confidence. But more returns judged only on the final refund still miss what the agent did along the way.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agent results can vary between runs. But repeated runs judged only on refunds still miss wrong emails and stock changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the refund is the end result. But the agent chose each email and stock change itself, and none of them was checked.

tips: Eliminate: A adds cases to a test that checks only refunds, and C assumes the agent's other actions were right because its refunds were.
Final two: D beats B because reviewing each tool action catches wrong emails and stock changes, while repeated runs still look only at refunds.
Exam cue: For an AI agent, acceptance covers the path as well as the result: every tool action and message it produces.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Photos supplied by applicants
questions.question: A Maltese passport office lets applicants upload their own photos, which border gates later match against travelers' faces. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: A printed photo held up to a border gate's camera
options.B: Poor lighting making genuine travelers fail to match
options.C: A blended photo letting two people match one passport
options.D: Applicants uploading photos taken several years earlier

questions.key_concept: Self-supplied enrollment photos allow morphing: one blended face that matches two people, so both can use one passport at a face-matching gate.
questions.pre_read: Rank the threats by likelihood and impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Because applicants supply their own photos, one can submit an image blended from two faces. Face matching can accept both people against it, so a second person can cross with the first's passport, and nothing looks wrong at the gate. A printed photo held to a gate camera is a known presentation attack, but gates can check for a live face, while the blended photo is genuine to the system.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because presentation attacks are well known. But they happen at a gate that can check for a live face; a blended enrollment photo needs no trick there.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lighting causes errors. But that is an accuracy problem with honest travelers, not an attack someone exploits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because old photos match poorly. But aging is an accuracy issue that causes refusals, not a way for someone to cross on another's passport.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe honest accuracy problems that cause refusals, not threats an attacker exploits.
Final two: C beats A because a blended photo is accepted as genuine at enrollment, while a printed photo must beat the gate's checks.
Exam cue: When people supply their own enrollment images, consider morphing attacks that let two faces share one identity.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Retiring a tuned telemedicine model
questions.question: When a Georgian telemedicine firm retired its model fine-tuned on consultation notes, engineers deleted the deployed model, the tuning data and backups of both. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Patients were not told that the model would be retired
options.B: Checkpoints saved during training may survive as model copies
options.C: Deleted files may still be recoverable from the storage disks
options.D: The vendor's base model may still hold the consultation notes

questions.key_concept: Training often saves checkpoints, each a model copy that may repeat training data; retirement finds every copy and records whether it is kept or deleted.
questions.pre_read: Think through the model's whole history before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning commonly saves checkpoints, each a full copy of the model at that stage, often in an experiment tracker apart from production. A tuned model can reproduce text from its training notes, so a surviving checkpoint carries the same patient data. Recovery from disks is a real sanitization point, but it takes forensic effort, while a checkpoint is a working copy anyone with access can run.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a transparency step. But nothing in the facts creates a duty to announce a retirement; leftover copies are the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a media-sanitization point. But disk remnants need forensic recovery, while a leftover checkpoint is a ready-to-run copy of the tuned model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tuning starts from a base model. But tuning changed a copy; the base model never saw the consultation notes.

tips: Eliminate: D forgets that tuning changes a copy, not the vendor's base model, and A invents a duty to tell patients about a retirement.
Final two: B beats C because a checkpoint is a ready-to-run copy that can repeat patient notes, while disk remnants need forensic recovery.
Exam cue: When a model trained on sensitive data is retired, find every copy, including training checkpoints and experiment records.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Plain-language rewrites
questions.question: A Slovak insurer accepted a model's plain-language policy rewrites after lawyers confirmed meaning was kept. Staff preferred the rewrites in 70% of 300 pairs labeled by version. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Score rewrites by word overlap with the original terms
options.B: Redo the comparison with raters not told which text is which
options.C: Accept it, since a 70% preference is a clear and decisive majority
options.D: Have a grading model rate the same 300 pairs instead

questions.key_concept: Human preference tests of generated output must hide which version produced each item, or labels can sway the judgments.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each stated result was produced.
questions.correct_explanation: Raters who know which rewrite is new can be swayed by that label, toward novelty or toward the familiar, so a preference count from labeled pairs may reflect the labels more than the text. Repeating the comparison blind gives a fair result. A grading model would not see the labels, but it brings leanings of its own, such as favoring longer text, and its marks count only once checked against people.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as an objective measure. But word overlap rewards copying the original, the opposite of a plain-language rewrite, and ignores meaning.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 70% looks decisive. But a clear majority from biased ratings is still biased.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a grading model never sees the labels. But grading models lean their own way, such as toward longer text, and need checking against people first.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a majority that may come from the labels, and A rewards copying the original wording, which plain language should change.
Final two: B beats D because a grading model swaps the label bias for leanings of its own; blind raters remove the bias and still judge as readers do.
Exam cue: When people judge generated output, hide which system produced it, or the judgment may test the label.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Longer uploads
questions.question: A Japanese machine-tool maker's portal assistant now accepts 500 pages of input, up from 10, so customers can upload specifications. Jailbreak tests passed before the change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the earlier tests, since the model itself is unchanged
options.B: Rerun the existing jailbreak tests on the changed assistant
options.C: Restrict uploaded pages to customers with signed contracts
options.D: Retest with jailbreaks built into long uploaded documents

questions.key_concept: Longer input limits allow many-shot jailbreaks that fill the input with fake examples of rule-breaking; tests must use the new lengths.
questions.pre_read: Restate the change in your own words.
questions.correct_explanation: Long inputs allow attacks short tests never try, such as many-shot jailbreaking: hundreds of fake exchanges in which the assistant breaks its rules, which can wear down its safeguards. The earlier tests used inputs that fit the old limit. Rerunning them on the changed assistant checks nothing new, because they are still short; tests must use the longer inputs the change now allows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model did not change. But the input limit changes what attackers can send, so earlier results no longer cover it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as standard retesting after a change. But the old tests are all short, so rerunning them cannot reveal attacks that need long inputs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a way to vet senders. But contracted customers can still send long jailbreaks, and their files can carry others' text.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes only model changes matter, though the limit changes what attackers can send, and C vets senders without testing what long inputs can do.
Final two: D beats B because the old tests never use long inputs; rerunning them cannot show whether the new limit opened an attack.
Exam cue: When a change widens what an AI accepts, test the new attacks it allows, not only the old suite.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Dispatch agent's tool keys
questions.question: A Kazakh trucking company's quarterly access review covers its dispatch agent's directory account; the agent calls booking and payment tools with API keys held in each tool. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rotate the tools' API keys every 30 days
options.B: Have each tool's owner review that tool's key rights quarterly
options.C: Include rights the agent holds through tool keys in the review
options.D: Accept the review, since the directory controls the agent's access

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's real access includes rights held through each tool's own credentials, which may sit outside the identity directory.
questions.pre_read: Picture how the agent completes one task.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent can do whatever its tools' keys allow, and here those keys sit in the tools, outside the directory the review covers, so the review misses its rights to book trucks and make payments. Per-tool reviews would see each key, but an agent chains its tools on its own, so only reviewing its rights together shows it can both book and pay for loads.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as good key hygiene. But rotating a key changes its secret, not what the key allows the agent to do.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as owner-based review. But each owner sees one key; only a review of the agent shows that it can both book trucks and pay for them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because directories usually hold access. But this agent's booking and payment rights come from keys stored in the tools.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the directory holds all of the agent's rights, and A changes the keys' secrets without checking what each key allows.
Final two: C beats B because an agent chains its tools, so its rights must be reviewed together; each tool's key can look fine alone.
Exam cue: An agent's real access is everything its tools' credentials allow; access reviews must cover them.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Export quotes after a devaluation
questions.question: After Sri Lanka's rupee fell 40% in a month, a Colombo rubber exporter's quote-pricing model began underquoting orders. Engineers plan to roll back to last year's approved version. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The rollback may overwrite evidence of the current version's fault
options.B: Last year's version also learned from prices before the fall
options.C: A rollback needs fresh approval from the change board
options.D: Last year's version may be slower at quoting each order

questions.key_concept: Rollback contains a faulty release, not drift; when conditions shift, earlier versions trained before the shift may fail the same way.
questions.pre_read: Note what each party in the stem plans to do.
questions.correct_explanation: The fault comes from a market shift, not a bad release: last year's version also learned from prices before the devaluation, so it would likely underquote orders the same way, and the rollback would contain nothing. Preserving the current version as evidence matters, but it can be saved before any switch; it does not make the plan stop the underquoting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because evidence matters in an incident. But the current version can be saved before any switch; the plan's flaw is that the older version would underquote too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as change discipline. But returning to an approved version is a planned containment step; the problem is that this version predates the fall too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a service point. But quoting speed is not the harm here; the older version's view of prices is.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a planned rollback to an approved version as needing fresh approval, and D worries about speed when the harm is underquoting.
Final two: B beats A because the older version predates the fall too, so the rollback stops nothing; evidence can be saved before any switch.
Exam cue: Before a rollback, ask whether the earlier version would fail the same way; drift affects every version trained before the shift.
